description:
Places like Delaney Hall are key material nodes of the deportation regime.
Readers will note that the architecture of the deportation regime described thus far was constructed mainly by the federal government.
Throughout these accounts, Washington emphasizes that resistance to the deportation regime must always propose alternative futures to counter the scapegoating drive of the deportation regime.
What can we fight for instead of the destructive deportation regime?
The deportation regime now pervades US society.
text:
How to Close a Camp: Dispatches from the Fight Against Immigrant Detention by John Washington . Haymarket Books , 2026. 272 pages.Buy on Bookshop.org

ANOTHER PERSON DIED in an ICE detention center. On Saturday, August 1, Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, a 41-year-old Salvadoran immigrant, was pronounced dead by medical workers at University Hospital in Newark, New Jersey, after being transported there from the Delaney Hall Detention Facility, which operates on behalf of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Lopez-Cornejo is the second Delaney Hall detainee to die in the past eight months. The conditions there are deplorable but not exceptional.

Detention facilities like the one where Lopez-Cornejo was caged are linchpins of contemporary white supremacy. Having gained control of state power in large part by stoking fears about a “Great Replacement” of the nation’s white majority by people of color, white supremacists in the United States are now setting about fulfilling their promise to restore the nation by massively amplifying their effort to purge the country of “illegal aliens.”

The crackdown on those deemed alien is not, in other words, simply about fulfilling Donald Trump’s pledge to secure the border. To purify the nation, the Trump regime needs a massive network of interdiction, detention, and deportation. It may seem an ironic predicament given the Right’s long aversion to state bureaucracy. But this isn’t about expanding the redistributive wing of the state—it’s about building a vast paramilitary apparatus to surveil every aspect of life across the nation. While less visible than the deadly paramilitary operations the Trump administration unleashed on cities like Minneapolis and Los Angeles, detention facilities like Delaney Hall are core elements of white supremacy—of what anthropologist Nicholas De Genova calls the deportation regime. After all, once people are rounded up, they must be locked away somewhere until they can be ejected from the body politic. Places like Delaney Hall are key material nodes of the deportation regime. They are also sites of ideological legitimation for the regime.

Yet these places are also crucibles of resistance, emanating both from those caged within and from the surrounding civil society. Last year, for instance, four people organized a successful escape from the Delaney Hall facility. This May, people detained there launched a hunger strike to protest bad medical care, dirty living quarters, and unsafe and insufficient meals. Hundreds of community members rallied outside. Some protesters tried to prevent ICE agents from entering and leaving the facility. Video subsequently went viral of protesters being bludgeoned by masked ICE agents and goons hired by GEO Group, the private prison corporation running Delaney Hall.

But it wasn’t just grassroots demonstrators whose bodies and rights were trampled on. Democratic elected officials were denied entry to Delaney Hall, and ICE agents arrested Newark mayor Ras Baraka for trespassing, charged Congresswoman LaMonica McIver with assaulting a federal officer, and pepper-sprayed Senator Andy Kim. Still, the Democratic establishment often cooperates with ICE. In fact, although local police initially kept their distance as protesters sought to disrupt business as usual at Delaney Hall, Baraka and New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill eventually deployed state police and local cops to assist ICE and corral the protesters. This collaboration has come under withering public attack. Local politicians have expressed increasing criticism of how Delaney Hall is being run. The death of Lopez-Cornejo is likely to intensify local political mobilization against ICE.

The events at Delaney Hall suggest that well-organized opposition—from both within and around detention centers—can seriously erode and even upend support for the deportation regime. To continue building a movement powerful enough not simply to shut down individual detention facilities like Delaney Hall but to abolish the entire deportation regime, activists need to understand who supports and who benefits from building cages for migrants. The movement also must develop a deep historical understanding of the deportation regime’s origins, ideological legitimation, and diverse modes of operation. And abolitionists need a keen strategic sense of the regime’s sites of vulnerability, the places where movements can apply political and economic pressure effectively. How does this pressure need to change at different historical moments? How can movements operate effectively at and across specific scales?

John Washington’s new book How to Close a Camp: Dispatches from the Fight Against Immigrant Detention is an essential manual for movements seeking to dismantle the core apparatuses of contemporary white supremacy. As Washington explains, the names for the sites where migrants are caged are legion, and their forms are heterogeneous: detention centers, processing centers, holding facilities, and a host of local jails and prison facilities around the United States and in many other countries, all of which are stitched into a vast, transnational deportation regime. How to Close a Camp aims to acknowledge this immense diversity while also providing an effective map of how ICE mobilizes across these different sites. The heterogeneity of detention makes for slipperiness. Indeed, part of the point is to keep significant sections of the public in the dark about this archipelago of cages by maintaining their relative invisibility. An important thrust of Washington’s book is to make the system visible. To close a camp, we must first understand what one looks like—not only physically but also juridically, economically, and even ideologically.

Early on, Washington offers readers a basic definition of the camp. It is more than just a prison or jail built or operated to lock up migrants, although it certainly is that. A camp is also, Washington suggests, an ideological operation of othering. It is “society seeing certain groups of people as unwanted and disposable.” It is a “distraction from entrenched political failure.” It is a refusal to take responsibility for and reckon with climate collapse, imperial war, and the economic dismantling of the welfare state. Drawing on other historians of the camp such as Harsha Walia, Giorgio Agamben, Silky Shah, Kelly Lytle Hernández, and A. Naomi Paik, Washington argues that the foundational logic of the camp is fear, hate, punishment, torture, banishment, and death.

Washington’s use of the term “camp” is clearly intended to conjure associations with the concentration and extermination camps operated by the Nazi regime. While there are important differences between Auschwitz and a place like Delaney Hall, such sites are of the same genus, Washington argues. In both places, caged people are rendered stateless, and thereby turned into dehumanized beings from whom, as Hannah Arendt famously argued, the “right to have rights” has been withdrawn. Once people are rendered superfluous in this manner, expulsion and even extermination are but a step away.

As Arendt intuited, the paradigm of the nation-state presupposes an excluded other. Citizenship in most nation-states was—and, in many, remains—defined by blood belonging. Even liberal nation-states such as the United States, where citizenship is not genetic, circumscribe belonging territorially, which means that they are always going to produce categories of people who do not belong. While the Nazi concentration camps are perhaps the most familiar examples of an apparatus designed to dehumanize and exterminate masses of people, a settler-colonial state like the US pioneered sites of confinement, exploitation, and dehumanization that served as precedents for the Nazis, including reservations for Native Americans and plantations for enslaved Africans.

Washington’s book acknowledges this history of colonial violence but focuses in most detail on the period since the late 19th century when the juridical and institutional order that underpins today’s deportation regime took shape. An early example the book explores, the Geary Act of 1892, required all people of Chinese origin in the United States to register with the federal government or be locked up. The measure passed a day before the adoption of the Chinese Exclusion Act. What followed was a series of crackdowns across the country that resulted in the locking up of Chinese Americans in what we can now see were early versions of today’s immigrant detention centers. Washington traces how these racist practices of detention and deportation were later amplified with the “internment” of roughly 120,000 people of Japanese descent during World War II.

Once these camps and the legal architectures that supported them were established, they offered a paradigm for subsequent efforts to cage people depicted as a threat to the nation. While Cold War competition with the Soviet Union pushed US authorities to temper somewhat the explicitly racist anti-immigrant politics of the early 20th century, the specter of communism also provided a rationale for new policies of detention and deportation. In 1952, for instance, Congress passed the Immigration and Nationality Act—also known as the McCarran-Walter Act. This legislation targeted immigrants suspected of subversive political activity, and the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) was duly ordered to deport anarchists and communists. In his discussion of these measures, Washington mentions how they led to the imprisonment of the great Trinidadian radical C. L. R. James on Ellis Island in New York, where he wrote his critical assessment of Moby-Dick (1851) as an allegory of the white supremacist republic. Contemporaneously with the McCarran-Walter Act, Operation Wetback intensified the racialization and criminalization of Mexican migrants, a key labor force during the postwar boom years.

These historical precedents form the foundation on which the deportation regime was established, but Washington correctly argues that the edifice we confront today was built out during the conservative counterrevolution of the 1980s and 1990s. In this period, the US carceral state was not only elaborated but also interlinked with what Washington calls “the camp.” In reaction to the civil rights and prisoner rights movements of the preceding decades, governing elites rolled out policies linking the war on crime, the war on immigrants, and the War on Terror. Supported by politicians from both political parties, these policies sought to stymie the efforts of prisoners and migrants to use habeas corpus and civil rights lawsuits to challenge mass detention and deportation.

How to Close a Camp emphasizes that today’s deportation regime has been a bipartisan construction. This is an important argument, one that needs underlining given the severity of the Trump administration’s crackdown on migrants. The point, though, is that this current assault is only possible as a result of the anti-immigrant machinations of the Democratic Party. For example, under the guise of cracking down on crime and terrorism, Democratic politicians including Joe Biden and Bill Clinton authored and supported laws such as the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA) and the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA), both passed in 1996. As Patrisia Macías-Rojas has pointed out in an important essay on these laws, AEDPA and IIRIRA did not use explicitly authoritarian language about mass detention; instead, they invoked civil rights ideals while simultaneously narrowing legal protections from detention, policing, deportation, and unchecked executive power.

In a parallel instance of this trend, then-representative Chuck Schumer of New York justified his Omnibus Counterterrorism Act of 1995 by arguing that “noncitizens do not, and should not, have rights.” This was flatly incorrect: constitutional protections apply to persons, not just to citizens. But Schumer’s legislation, which targeted “alien terrorists” in the United States for providing “material support” to organizations that opposed US support for Israel, provided a justification for using the immigration system as a weapon against anyone framed as a domestic terrorist. It is a bitter historical irony that Schumer’s legislation, intended to attack pro-Palestine activism, was legitimated by the bombing of a federal building in Oklahoma by white supremacist Timothy McVeigh, a veteran of the United States’ wars in the Middle East.

Readers will note that the architecture of the deportation regime described thus far was constructed mainly by the federal government. As Trump’s explicit framing of ICE as a force of occupation in majority-Democratic cities like Minneapolis makes clear, it is undeniably true that anti-migrant laws and institutions have been facilitated by the so-called plenary power of the executive branch. But the key point of Washington’s book is that none of these measures could be successfully implemented without local cooperation. The deportation regime, How to Close a Camp demonstrates, is multiscalar. This is not simply a theoretical point; it has very real strategic implications. To fight the deportation regime successfully, activists must continue resisting the ways local authorities collaborate with ICE and the many corporations growing fat off contracts provided by the federal government. As Washington puts it, we must understand something:

[I]mmigration detention camps are not abstract federal machines. They are, rather, deeply embedded in local political economies: counties that sign contracts with ICE, private prison companies that seek zoning permits and tax breaks, local health departments that license medical providers, and municipal governments that issue permits for food services and utility hookups. Every one of these nodes is a potential pressure point.

At a moment when every branch of the federal government has been captured by authoritarian forces, the movement can notch up victories on local and state levels.

Telling stories about how things unfolded in specific exemplary towns, How to Close a Camp explains that detention centers are sold to local authorities and communities as a form of rural revitalization. Elected officials in small towns hit by decades of job losses and economic abandonment can be vulnerable to the siren song of representatives from corporations, who turn up with slick presentations promising loads of well-paying jobs and inflated local tax revenues. But, as Washington explains, these promises turn out to be hollow: profiteering corporations give contracts to build and operate the camps to the lowest bidders, a process that cuts local businesses out even as local tax budgets are strained and public health resources groan under the medical crises bred by the camps. Washington effectively demonstrates how the resulting local crises are sutured into the extreme inequalities that characterize contemporary capitalism. Indeed, 90 percent of detainees in the United States are locked in camps run by private, for-profit corporations like GEO Group and CoreCivic, which in turn are bankrolled by massive investment management companies such as BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street. While wealth investors get even richer by warehousing migrants, local towns see their budgets go bust. Even those who get jobs in the camps often end up struggling with debilitating forms of PTSD after years spent enforcing inhumane conditions. Camps turn out to be a scam rather than a winning lottery ticket.

Washington lays out the ways movements in various parts of the country have fought back. Activists have learned how to scrutinize municipal budgets, zoning regulations, and laws. People such as Fred Tsao have fought successfully for legislation like Illinois’s Way Forward Act (2021), which prohibits state and local governments from engaging in federal immigration enforcement. The book deftly weaves together specific stories like Tsao’s and broader lessons for the movement. How to Close a Camp also discusses resistance to ICE surges by neighborhood organizations like Lucha Zapoteca in Los Angeles, which developed potent networks of mutual aid and self-defense that helped turn back the deportation regime’s surge into the city.

Throughout these accounts, Washington emphasizes that resistance to the deportation regime must always propose alternative futures to counter the scapegoating drive of the deportation regime. Movements cannot simply focus on fighting back against ICE and detention centers. Abolition requires a positive vision. What do local communities need? What can we fight for instead of the destructive deportation regime? If municipal budgets are not funneled into providing tax breaks for corporations like GEO Group, how might the resulting public funding be used to support things like universal childcare?

Proving true to its optimistic title, How to Close a Camp provides a host of specific case studies and concrete suggestions about how to fight the deportation regime. Washington’s book offers hope in a very dark moment: if camps are built on layers of local business and bureaucratic transactions, each of these is a point of complicity and possible weakness. But breaking the collaboration of local elites is a very tough task. This complicity is mobilized by measures such as the 287(g) program, which deputizes local law enforcement to assist ICE by handing over people in jails or by patrolling in search of migrants. Even in the absence of such programs, local cops often collaborate with federal authorities. In research conducted for his 2025 book On the Side of ICE: Policing Immigrants in a Sanctuary State, anthropologist Peter Mancina examined body camera footage of local police departments’ encounters with immigrants and federal agents in New Jersey, a supposed sanctuary state despite the existence of now notorious facilities like Delaney Hall. Mancina’s analysis documents how local police serve as a force multiplier by assisting ICE voluntarily, even while the cops are complying with sanctuary laws. As Mancina’s work stresses, the institutional culture of the cops—and the legal infrastructure that prevents them from being held accountable—must change to prevent police from targeting Brown and Black people for immigration enforcement.

We face deepening crisis conditions. Edwin Lopez-Cornejo was not the only person to die this year in a camp. So far in 2026, there have been 24 deaths in ICE custody. Rights groups like Human Rights Watch and the ACLU report that the mortality rate in ICE facilities has reached its highest level in over a decade, driven by a record-high expansion of detentions. The Trump regime has turned over truly staggering quantities of taxpayer money to ICE. This deluge of funding is having an impact. ICE agents arrested a record 43,138 people in June, according to analysis of the latest ICE records. The deportation regime now pervades US society. As Washington puts it near the close of his book, “The threat of the camp is not idle, abstract, or in the future. It is now. While the threat is concentrated on otherized populations, anybody and everybody is a target. You are a target.”

So what are you going to do?

LARB Contributor

Ashley Dawson is a distinguished professor at the City University of New York. He is the author, most recently, of Environmentalism from Below: How Global People’s Movements Are Leading the Fight for Our Planet (Haymarket Books, 2024) and co-editor of Decolonize Conservation: Global Voices for Indigenous Self-Determination, Land, and a World in Common (Common Notions, 2023).

text:
A man who says he was badly injured during an immigration arrest on Columbia Pike is demanding a criminal investigation.

Protesters gathered outside the Arlington County Justice Center this morning (Friday) in support of Jose Mejia Hernandez, who says he suffered a brain bleed and other injuries after Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers reportedly chased him and shot him with a Taser earlier this month.

Mejia Hernandez’s counsel filed a police report seeking a criminal investigation from the Arlington County Police Department. They planned to meet with investigators today to discuss Mejia Hernandez’s arrest on Aug. 11 in a parking lot in an apartment complex at Columbia Pike and S. Courthouse Road.

Attorney Denisse Gastélum described Mejia Hernandez fleeing from masked officers who approached him without warning. She also shared two videos from bystanders that show immigration enforcement tending to injuries on her client’s face immediately after the incident.

“As he’s walking to the bus stop, he recalls strangers approaching,” Gastélum said. “He didn’t know who they were. He didn’t recognize them. They didn’t look like police officers. He was concerned and he started running.”

Mejia Hernandez has said that he has a gap in his memory between getting hit with a stun gun and waking up in a hospital bed. He says that he lost consciousness, although bystander video of the incident shows him sitting upright and ultimately standing up, surrounded by ICE agents.

Carlos Jurado, Mejia Hernandez’s immigration attorney, said that he has many unanswered questions about ICE officers’ actions during the incident, although he says his client suffered a traumatic brain injury resulting in brain swelling and a brain bleed.

“What did they do? I have no idea,” Jurado said. “That’s why we’re here. We’re trying to piece it together.”

In a letter to ACPD, Gastélum alleged that witnesses reported Mejia Hernandez being struck by an officer’s vehicle while he was on foot. However, available videos only show the aftermath of whatever happened.

The Department of Homeland Security told HuffPost that Mejia Hernandez is undocumented and that he “attempted to flee from the scene, requiring ICE to use necessary force to gain control of the situation.”

“Allegations that he was unconscious and woke up in a hospital bed are FALSE,” the agency said. “According to officers, they rendered aid, asked the individual, who was responsive, if he was okay after evading arrest, and followed their training.”

Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti told ARLnow that ACPD “has been examining available information concerning this incident” and that “the filing of a police report is a catalyst for a more robust investigation.”

“ACPD does not participate in federal immigration enforcement, and our Trust Policy prohibits initiating contact with ICE,” de Ferranti said. “Although the law does not permit the County to interfere or intervene in ICE operations, we are and will do everything we can within the law to provide support and to protect the safety of all our residents, documented and undocumented.”

Commonwealth’s Attorney Parisa Dehghani-Tafti also delivered brief remarks at the press conference, saying that she supports “a full investigation.”

“Without pre-judging what the results of this investigation will be, it is absolutely necessary to send a message that nobody is above the law,” Dehghani-Tafti said.

Dehghani-Tafti added in a press release that she “has been working behind the scenes” to facilitate a meeting with ACPD detectives and support Mejia Hernandez through victim/witness advocates.

Mejia Hernandez said in Spanish that in the weeks after the incident, his brain injury has prevented him from going to work and affected his ability to eat, sleep and form sentences.

In addition to seeking a criminal investigation, attorneys are pursuing a U visa, a form of documentation for victims of certain crimes, along with civil litigation against the U.S. government.

Mejia Hernandez’s detainment took place amid a large-scale ICE operation in the D.C. area that resulted in the arrests of over 1,300 people, according to the Department of Homeland Security. It is unclear how many of these were in Arlington.

“How does a man walking to a bus stop on his way to work end up bleeding from his brain after an encounter with ICE?” Gastélum and Jurado wrote in a press release. “Mr. Mejia Hernandez deserves that answer. The public does too.”

title: We Cannot Allow ICE Killings to Become Normal | Common Dreams
description:
His death marks more than 50 deaths in ICE custody since President Donald Trump took office last year.
Despite all the controversies, ICE keeps killing people—a sentence that should never feel normal.
This summer it was Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.
According to his family’s attorney, Durán Guerrero was lawfully present in the United States and had a work permit.
ICE deaths reached their highest level in decades last year, and this year is on track to be no better.
text:
Jose Chajon-Raxon, an immigrant from Guatemala, died this August at Delaney Hall, a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in New Jersey. His death marks more than 50 deaths in ICE custody since President Donald Trump took office last year.

Despite all the controversies, ICE keeps killing people—a sentence that should never feel normal. We should never find ourselves counting the days between deaths or waiting for the next headline. But somehow, we have.

Earlier this year it was Renee Good, then Alex Pretti. This summer it was Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero. Before them were Silviero Villegas Gonzalez and Ruben Ray Martinez. Those are only the names we know—many others will never make national news.

The day I read about Durán Guerrero’s death, I was returning home from work. I glanced at the headline and kept going. That’s what scared me the most. I wasn’t shocked that ICE had killed someone—I expected it.

No matter where you were born, what political party you belong to, or whether you support stricter immigration enforcement, no government should have the power to kill or imprison people with so little accountability.

Only later, when I stopped and read the details, did it hit me: He was shot multiple times. His 3-year-old daughter, wearing Bluey pajamas, was in the car when it happened. According to his family’s attorney, Durán Guerrero was lawfully present in the United States and had a work permit. And he wasn’t even the person ICE was looking for when he was shot.

After shooting Durán Guerrero, officers pulled him from the vehicle and handcuffed him. By then, he may already have been dead.

These are not tragic misunderstandings. These are choices.

Imagine seeing armed people in tactical gear—no body cam, their faces covered—surrounding your car. Most people would be terrified. Most people would try to get away. Durán Guerrero tried to stop, but it did not matter—the agents fired on him anyway.

ICE continues carrying out operations with masked agents in unmarked vehicles, creating confusion and fear before a single word is spoken. Immigration officers have fired on at least 30 people since President Trump returned to office. Eight of those people were killed.

Each time, the government tells us the agents acted in self-defense. Public statements quickly frame the victim as the threat. Witness testimony and video evidence often cast doubt on these accounts, but they still shift the focus away from the loss of human life and toward justifying why it happened.

Meanwhile, tens of thousands of people are still being detained every month.

In June 2026, ICE arrested more than 43,000 people, about 1,400 every day. By July, nearly 68,000 people were being held in immigration detention. The overwhelming majority of those arrested had no criminal convictions.

This includes over 6,000 children. Children who are spending their birthdays behind bars. Children who should be back in school, safe and protected. Many have been detained for 100 days or more—five times longer than the 20-day limit for detaining immigrant children.

They’re being held in facilities like Delaney and others, where human rights groups have warned repeatedly that dangerous conditions are leading to preventable deaths. ICE deaths reached their highest level in decades last year, and this year is on track to be no better.

These numbers matter. Every statistic was someone’s father, daughter, husband, neighbor, friend.

I’m afraid of how easy it has become to read another headline and move on. I know because I caught myself doing exactly that.

No matter where you were born, what political party you belong to, or whether you support stricter immigration enforcement, no government should have the power to kill or imprison people with so little accountability. No family should have to watch a loved one become another name on a growing list.

We cannot allow these deaths to become routine, and we cannot let them disappear into statistics. Every death should force us to ask what kind of country we are becoming. We cannot normalize these killings, and we cannot stop demanding justice and accountability.

We should never get used to counting ICE’s victims.

text:
Today’s ruling from the Third Circuit is the eighth from a federal appeals court to find the policy unlawful

August 28, 2026 2:30 pm

PHILADEPHIA — Another federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration’s new policy subjecting millions of immigrants to mandatory detention without access to bond hearings.

Today’s ruling from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit stems from a lawsuit brought by the American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Pennsylvania, ACLU of New Jersey, and the law firm of Palladino, Isbell & Casazza, LLC. The case is Buele Morocho v. Warden Philadelphia FDC.

The Third Circuit decision joins similar rulings from seven other federal appeals courts and hundreds of district court judges in finding the policy unlawful.

For decades, immigrants in removal proceedings who were detained by the government have generally had the right to seek release by an immigration judge. In mid-2025, the Trump administration suddenly adopted a new radical reinterpretation of the immigration laws and declared that anyone who entered without inspection must be detained without access to bond.

Among those who were affected were people eligible for legal status, even those with long-pending immigration applications who have been waiting years due to administrative backlogs.

The following is reaction to today’s ruling:

“The courts have repeatedly and resoundingly rejected the Trump administration’s radical reinterpretation of our country’s detention laws. This ruling is another critical victory against the administration’s cruelty and disrespect for the rule of law. We are thrilled for our clients and their families,” said Michael Tan, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project.

“Even before the Trump administration began its campaign to detain every person it could round up, immigration detention was a cruel and unnecessary practice,” said Vanessa Stine, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Pennsylvania. “But denying bond hearings to the individuals ICE detains is an alarming trend that is blatantly at odds with the plain text of the statute and the Constitution’s guarantee of due process. We applaud today’s decision and look forward to continuing the fight to end the Trump administration’s dangerous and unconstitutional targeting of immigrant communities.”

“This ruling underscores that this administration cannot make up its own rules in order to lock up huge numbers of people without a bond hearing,” said Farrin Anello, senior counsel for the ACLU of New Jersey. “We applaud the court’s careful and painstaking analysis of the statutes in question and its conclusion that the government must follow the plain language of the law and the Constitution in order to take away someone’s freedom. Today is a win for immigrants’ rights and the rule of law.”

“Within the Third Circuit, this decision puts an end to a year-long campaign by the administration to indefinitely detain human beings without due process. We feel incredibly fortunate to have co-counseled with this legal team on this case," said Christopher M. Casazza, attorney with Palladino, Isbell & Casazza, LLC.

title: Racist 'Magic Deportation Bus' isn't the way for Trump to keep Latino voters - LA Times
description:
Bracketing this soulless scene are the words “The Magic Deportation Bus” — get it?
But this one was so bad that it even offended Martinez Valladares, a Republican whose district stretches from the Grapevine to Victorville.
Being tough on illegal immigration doesn’t require turning Latinos into a caricature.” Martinez Valladares isn’t any random Trump supporter.
“Take a ride on The Magic School Bus to your home country!” the White House spokesperson began.
But there’s one thing their putrid parody of “The Magic School Bus” got right.
text:
If you want proof of the widening chasm between the Trump administration and Latinos, look no further than California state Sen. Suzette Martinez Valladares and White House spokesperson Lauren Bis’ reaction to the same anti-Latino image.

Posted on the White House’s social media accounts this week, it’s a take on the logo for the beloved 1990s PBS cartoon “The Magic School Bus.” Same cheery font, same yellow bus blasting through the cosmos, same depiction of wacky teacher Ms. Frizzle and her cute chameleon sidekick Liz. But instead of a bunch of happy kids off to another adventure, the passengers are five handcuffed, brown-skinned, mustachioed men looking downward and dejected, all identical save for the colors of their T-shirts.

Bracketing this soulless scene are the words “The Magic Deportation Bus” — get it? Har har! The White House released the illustration to accompany an Aug. 24 Fox News headline gushing that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had arrested a “jaw-dropping number” of undocumented immigrants in the D.C. area over the last two weeks.

The post was the latest in a flood of racist, anti-immigrant images that the Trump administration has shared. But this one was so bad that it even offended Martinez Valladares, a Republican whose district stretches from the Grapevine to Victorville.

“Enforcing immigration law and securing the border isn’t anti-Latino. But this image wasn’t necessary or helpful,” she told me. “We can strongly support border security while expecting our government to communicate those policies without reducing a community to a stereotype. Being tough on illegal immigration doesn’t require turning Latinos into a caricature.”

Martinez Valladares isn’t any random Trump supporter. She’s co-chair of the California Hispanic Caucus, which represents the state’s GOP Latino legislators and was founded after a record number of them — nine — were elected in 2024. The group’s creation reflected the tsunami of Latino support for Trump that helped sweep him into the Oval Office for a second round and upended political thinking about America’s largest minority.

Such a critique from a politician of Martinez Valladares’ stature should set off fire alarms in the Oval Office as the midterms loom and the GOP needs Trump’s Latino supporters to hold the party line, right?

Nope!

When I asked the White House whether the “Magic Deportation Bus” was anti-Latino, spokesperson Bis whined in a statement that my query was “more race baiting by the media who are just mad the White House’s social media content is driving conversations with the American people about deporting illegal aliens. Is the L.A. Times really suggesting there has never been a deportation flight of just Guatemalans?”

Who’s doing the race baiting?

Nothing in the gross graphic suggests that Guatemala is the final destination for Migra Ms. Frizzle and her detainees. The men’s appearance is the only indication that they’re Latino — just the type of racial profiling that Trump’s immigration goons swear they don’t engage in, despite ample video and audio evidence to the contrary. While Latinos have long made up the majority of deportees, to portray the bus passengers as interchangeable clones who “look” Latino is as dehumanizing as you can get — but that’s par for MAGA.

Not only that, but the Fox News story that went with the icky illo said that ICE’s D.C. operation nabbed Jamaicans, Hondurans and Salvadorans, in addition to Guatemalans.

Trump and his minions famously never apologize, doubling down on their pendejadas when confronted with facts. Well, if Republicans wants any chance of holding on to Congress in the midterms and winning other key races, they need to beg Latinos for forgiveness, now that Trump has upended the lives of brown-skinned people, immigrants and U.S.-born alike.

Nearly half of Latinos voted for Trump two years ago, the best result ever for a Republican presidential candidate. Poll after poll released this year, each more dire for Trump than the last, show that those days are as distant a memory as affordable groceries. His approval ratings — and GOP hopes for the midterms — will continue to wither until he spends more time fixing the stagnant economy, ending the quagmire in Iran and stopping the deportation deluge.

To maintain his grip on power, Trump needs to inspire Latinos to stand by him, vote for his agenda and urge others to follow along. Instead, he faces frustrated supporters like David Hernandez, founder and chair of the Los Angeles County Hispanic Republican Club and host of the club’s weekly talk radio show.

Hernandez said he’s seen the perils of “unchecked” immigration at overcrowded hospitals and clinics. He also feels that in the race for California governor, Republican Steve Hilton’s attacks on Democrat Xavier Becerra’s alleged mishandling of migrant children while Health and Human Services secretary for the Biden administration will stay on the “front burner.”

The “Magic Deportation Bus” does nothing to highlight these issues, Hernandez said, describing it as “an immature cartoon failing to make any valid point.” Worse, the Navy veteran argues, it suggests that immigration agents plan to snatch children from schools.

“There is nothing funny about the issue,” Hernandez added, “that warrants this type of frivolous portrayal.”

I ran Hernandez’s and Martinez Valladares’ thoughts by Bis, noting their GOP bona fides without identifying them by name.

“Take a ride on The Magic School Bus to your home country!” the White House spokesperson began. Only her heart knows whether the line was a callback to the offending social media post or a not-nice suggestion that I self-deport to wherever the hell she thinks I was born (I’m a native Anaheimer, by the way).

Bis went on to repeat her previous line that the Trump administration is just seeking to “innovate” conversations with Americans and that “our efforts to deport criminal illegal aliens are no exception to this.”

Way to listen to the concerns of the front-line soldiers your boss so desperately needs this November, Lauren!

Spending more time crafting weak-salsa anti-Latino jokes than improving the lives of Latinos — that’s the racist swamp the president and his team happily fester in.

But there’s one thing their putrid parody of “The Magic School Bus” got right.

Ms. Frizzle often shrank her steel steed and its occupants to microscopic sizes so they could explore places they’d never seen. That sure sounds like the historic collapse that Trump is experiencing with Latinos, no?

To use Ms. Frizzle’s catchphrase: Bus, do your stuff.

title: Trump's New Birthright Citizenship Order Stays in Place as Judge Questions Constitutionality
description:
The Supreme Court first considered the litigation in 2025 in a dispute over universal injunctions, without deciding whether Trump’s citizenship policy itself violated the Constitution.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh provided a sixth vote to affirm the judgment but concluded that the order violated federal citizenship law rather than the Constitution.
Trump’s order reaches beyond those categories, including some foreign government employees and members of designated foreign terrorist organizations or people classified as specially designated global terrorists.
The plaintiffs include CASA, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project and families involved in the earlier birthright citizenship litigation.
Friday’s ruling leaves Trump’s new birthright citizenship order in place for now.
text:
President Donald Trump’s new order restricting birthright citizenship remained in effect Friday after a federal judge declined to immediately block it, while raising questions about whether the president can create new citizenship exceptions following a recent Supreme Court ruling.

U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland denied immigrant-rights advocates’ request for a temporary restraining order on Aug. 28 because their existing lawsuit challenges Trump’s earlier 2025 birthright citizenship directive and has not yet been amended to address the order he signed Aug. 6.

Boardman allowed the plaintiffs to update their complaint and set an expedited schedule for another challenge to the administration’s policy.

“As far as I can tell, this is unprecedented,” Boardman said during Friday’s hearing, according to Reuters. She described the new directive as an attempt to create exceptions to birthright citizenship “with the stroke of a pen.”

The dispute is the latest stage of a constitutional fight that began on Trump’s first day back in office and has already reached the Supreme Court over both the power of lower courts to block presidential policies nationwide and the meaning of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause.

Trump’s January 2025 executive order sought to deny automatic citizenship to children born in the United States when their mothers were unlawfully present or temporarily in the country and their fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

Boardman was among several federal judges who blocked that directive. The litigation later produced a nationwide class covering children who would be denied citizenship under the policy.

The Supreme Court first considered the litigation in 2025 in a dispute over universal injunctions, without deciding whether Trump’s citizenship policy itself violated the Constitution.

The constitutional question reached the justices the following year in Trump v. Barbara. On June 30, the Court affirmed a ruling against Trump’s 2025 order.

Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for a five-justice majority, held that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are “subject to the jurisdiction” of the United States and are citizens at birth under the Fourteenth Amendment. Justice Brett Kavanaugh provided a sixth vote to affirm the judgment but concluded that the order violated federal citizenship law rather than the Constitution.

The ruling traced birthright citizenship to the common-law principle of jus soli, or citizenship based on place of birth, and relied heavily on the Supreme Court’s 1898 decision in United States v. Wong Kim Ark.

Under that framework, people temporarily present in the United States generally remain subject to U.S. law, meaning children born to them on American soil qualify for citizenship. The Court recognized narrow historical exceptions involving people outside the ordinary jurisdiction of the United States, including foreign diplomats and enemies present during a hostile military occupation.

The Supreme Court also noted that foreigners who traveled to the United States for “business or pleasure” remained subject to American jurisdiction while in the country and that children born to them were citizens.

Trump responded five weeks later with Executive Order 14418, titled “Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship.”

Rather than again denying citizenship based broadly on a parent’s immigration status, the Aug. 6 order identifies narrower categories that the administration argues fall outside the constitutional rule recognized by the Supreme Court.

The directive applies when neither parent is a U.S. citizen and certain additional circumstances are present. It directs federal agencies not to recognize citizenship for some children whose parents are classified as “alien enemies,” children of certain foreign government employees and children whose parents allegedly used fraud or commercial arrangements to obtain birthright citizenship.

The order also targets what the administration calls “birth tourism,” including commercial arrangements intended to ensure that a mother gives birth in the United States. It covers some arrangements involving surrogates and births in U.S. territories where citizenship is not otherwise conferred by federal law.

Its foreign-government category extends beyond ambassadors to include certain embassy and consular employees, people working for foreign governments in an official capacity and some employees of international organizations.

The White House argues the new order follows the Supreme Court’s June ruling rather than conflicts with it. The administration points to the Court’s discussion of people who historically fell outside ordinary U.S. jurisdiction, including diplomats protected by immunity.

Boardman focused on that issue Friday when questioning Justice Department lawyers about birth tourism.

She asked where the Supreme Court’s June decision created an exception for children whose parents traveled to the United States for the purpose of giving birth. The Court had said temporary visitors remained subject to U.S. jurisdiction and cited historical authority involving foreigners who entered for “business or pleasure.”

Trump’s broader treatment of foreign government employees and “alien enemies” could raise similar questions.

The traditional exception for children of diplomats is tied to diplomatic immunity, while the historical enemy exception involves births during hostile military occupation. Trump’s order reaches beyond those categories, including some foreign government employees and members of designated foreign terrorist organizations or people classified as specially designated global terrorists.

Those differences are likely to become central when the court considers a direct challenge to the Aug. 6 order.

The Justice Department urged Boardman not to act immediately, arguing that federal agencies have not completed guidance explaining how the new policy will be implemented.

Trump directed the Departments of State, Justice and Homeland Security, the Social Security Administration and other federal agencies to bring their policies into line with the order and issue public implementation guidance within 30 days. That guidance is due by Sept. 5.

Boardman indicated Friday that she was reluctant to delay consideration of the constitutional questions until those instructions are released.

The plaintiffs include CASA, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project and families involved in the earlier birthright citizenship litigation. Their lawsuit previously resulted in certification of a class of children affected by Trump’s 2025 directive.

A separate challenge to the Aug. 6 order is also developing in the New Hampshire litigation that led to the Supreme Court’s decision in Trump v. Barbara. Plaintiffs there contend that the administration’s new restrictions reach people covered by the citizenship rule the Court affirmed in June.

Friday’s ruling leaves Trump’s new birthright citizenship order in place for now. It does not decide whether the restrictions are constitutional.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is planning to spend up to $2 million on robot “dogs” to assist its agents’ operations, according to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funding document.

A funding document posted to DHS’s Acquisition Planning Forecast System on Thursday said the agency could spend between $1 million and $2 million on Boston Dynamics’ “Spot” robot and accessories.

A senior DHS official confirmed the plans to NBC News and told the outlet that the robots will not be used to make arrests. The Hill has reached out to ICE for comment.

The technology is already in use by several law enforcement agencies, including the Los Angeles and New York police departments. The U.S. Secret Service also previously used the robotic dogs to secure President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago home in 2024.

These robots are equipped with cameras and sensors that can detect vibration, gas and radiation, according to Boston Dynamics.

In the government funding notice description, the agency said these robots will allow for “inspection, situational awareness, and hazard assessment in environments that may pose risks to personnel.”

“This capability helps improve officer safety, supports informed operational decision-making, and enhances DHS’s ability to respond to incidents involving dangerous, confined, unstable, or difficult-to-access areas,” the notice states.

Boston Dynamics said in its ethics statement that it “will not authorize nor partner with those who wish to use our robots as weapons or autonomous targeting systems.”

“If our products are being used for harm, we will take appropriate measures to mitigate that misuse,” the company continued.

This new proposal follows the agency’s controversial decision earlier this month to purchase as much as $20 million worth of electric shock gloves for officers to wear during immigration operations. White House border czar Tom Homan defended the move against criticism, arguing the gloves would prevent agents from needing to resort to deadly force.

text:
An Indian migrant jailed for robbing a grandmother and a young mother of their jewellery has been allowed to remain in the UK because it would be “devastating” for his wife if he were deported.

The man was sentenced to five years for robbing a “vulnerable” grandmother of her gold chain while she waited at a bus stop, and snatching a gold necklace from a woman who was walking with her children in a pram.

During the first of the robberies, which he committed while on drugs, the grandmother fell to the ground and suffered cuts and grazes, an immigration tribunal heard.

But the tribunal judge found it would be “unduly harsh” to deport the man, who has two children with his wife, a British citizen.

India ‘too dangerous’ for family

The judge heard it would be too dangerous for his family to travel with him if he were deported, because of threats allegedly made by family members, and his wife, who suffers from a rare form of inflammatory arthritis as well as mental health issues, would be “devastated” to lose him.

Despite his crimes, the tribunal in Birmingham granted his appeal on human rights grounds against deportation.

The Indian, who cannot be named for legal reasons but was referred to as AB, came to the UK when he was 11, after his father was jailed in the UK for murdering his mother in an arson attack.

In 2017, he met and married his wife, who is of Pakistani origin, and although he had been brought up a Sikh, he converted to Islam.

The tribunal was told this caused upset in both families, with “threats” being made against both of them, including that if they moved to India, a prominent Pakistani politician relative would kill them.

AB was convicted in 2017 of assault occasioning actual bodily harm of a man and a woman when he was drunk, and he was given a suspended sentence of 12 months.

Two years later, he was convicted of the two robberies, and was jailed for five years.

Wife’s serious medical conditions

Judge Anna-Rose Landes said the migrant was a “serious offender” because he had been jailed for more than four years, which meant there was a “greater public interest in deporting [him]”.

But she noted he had made progress towards rehabilitation since the offences were committed, indicating that he had “tried to get his life back on course by the stage of sentence”.

The court was told his wife (identified as CD) suffers from multiple medical conditions, including depression, palindromic rheumatism, fibromyalgia, anxiety and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome. Her husband is her main carer, and also the primary carer for their two children when she is unable to fulfil that role.

Judge Landes said: “Drawing everything together, I have found it would be beyond unduly harsh, indeed devastating, for CD to be separated from [AB].

“The effect on her of separation and the separation from their father, who has been the parent mainly responsible for their care, will lead to unduly harsh consequences for the children ... The best interests of the children lie very strongly in their remaining in the UK with [him].

“I am satisfied that that very strong public interest [in deporting him] is outweighed and there are very compelling circumstances over and above those described in the exceptions.”

title: 'My whole world stopped': How a routine ICE check-in upended a Syrian-American family
description:
Her father, Iemad Saifo, had received a letter telling him to present himself for a "check-in".
A few minutes later, the lawyer returned and told the family that ICE was detaining him.
A wider ICE crackdown Iemad's detention came as ICE has expanded its enforcement activity across the US.
ICE defended Iemad's detention by pointing to his lack of permanent immigration status and his witness-tampering conviction.
Now that Iemad is home, Zena said the family is grateful to the people who helped them through the ordeal.
text:
When Zena Saifo arrived at a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) office in New Jersey with her father, she expected a routine appointment.

Her father, Iemad Saifo, had received a letter telling him to present himself for a "check-in".

At the time, he believed he had little reason to worry; he had been working with his lawyers on his immigration case and had been complying with the requirements placed upon him.

The family knew immigrants were being detained across the United States, but they didn't expect Iemad to be taken into custody.

They arrived at an ICE office in Mount Laurel at 7.30am on 31 July for his 8am appointment. They waited several hours before an officer asked Iemad if he had any medication with him.

"That's when I kind of started to question - is he going to be detained?" Zena told Middle East Eye.

Soon after, Iemad was called to the back of the office with his lawyer. A few minutes later, the lawyer returned and told the family that ICE was detaining him.

Zena asked that she at least be allowed to say goodbye, but her request was denied.

"I just felt like my whole world had stopped," the 27-year-old told MEE. "My heart dropped to my stomach."

Iemad, a 65-year-old Syrian immigrant and father of four, would spend roughly two weeks in ICE detention before an immigration judge released him on bond on 15 August.

For his family, the detention was not only a legal battle. It became a race against time to bring their father home.

'Whole world stopped'

Iemad came to the US from Syria in 2002 on a B-1/B-2 joint business/tourism visa and eventually opened Zena's American Mediterranean Cuisine in Collingswood, New Jersey, along with other businesses.

His wife and children have US citizenship, and his family have pursued legal avenues to obtain permanent residency for him.

His immigration history, however, is complicated.

According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Iemad's visa expired in May 2002. An immigration judge ordered him removed in September 2010, but the case was reopened in January 2011.

In February 2023, an immigration judge administratively closed his removal case.

Iemad also has a criminal conviction. DHS has described him as a "criminal illegal alien" and said he was convicted of witness tampering.

'My whole world had stopped,'

Zena Saifo

Court records reviewed by WHYY, a public media organisation, show he pleaded guilty to the offence and was sentenced to five years' probation, 100 hours of community service, a fine and restitution.

DHS has also referred to previous arrests for theft by deception and identity impersonation.

Zena has rejected the characterisation of her father and described him as "a pillar of our family and our community". She said that since he moved to the US, he has sought legal pathways to citizenship.

"Our family should not be torn apart because of a nearly decade-old single non-violent offence - my father did what was asked of him and since then has focused on his family, his restaurant and his community."

Iemad has also disputed the way the government has described his immigration status. In an interview after his release, he said he had been pursuing permanent residency through his US citizen family and was waiting for an interview.

"I am pending, I am compliant, and I'm waiting for my interview," he said.

His lawyer, Fiona Powell, said Iemad was eligible to seek bond because of the circumstances of his immigration case and his history in the US.

During his detention, more than 150 people, including family members and community supporters, wrote and notarised letters vouching for Iemad's character and urging the judge to release him.

His lawyers and family also gathered thousands of petition signatures and letters of support from local elected officials and community organisations.

Powell said the community support was significant during the bond hearing, with the judge citing Iemad's strong community ties in deciding to release him.

'There was no humanity'

While he was detained, Iemad said he was handcuffed at his wrists and ankles and had his hands chained to his waist.

"We [the detainees in transport] waited about 30 hours," he said. "A human line, but a person doesn't feel like a human. There was no humanity in the treatment."

He said he went roughly two days without sleep while detainees were packed into rooms where illnesses quickly spread.

Iemad also said he had difficulty obtaining some of the medication he takes regularly, after one portion of his medication was not entered into the detention centre's computer system.

"I asked to see the doctor," he said. "They told me I would see him soon, but those were empty words."

He said that by the time he was released, he was exhausted and felt physically weak.

Zena said her father lost roughly 15 pounds (6.8kg) during his detention, and that a pre-existing voice condition worsened after he missed medication and experienced poor living conditions. After he returned home, she said, he spent several days mostly sleeping and recovering.

For Zena, some of the most difficult moments came while her father was still detained and she had little idea what was happening to him.

Over the phone, she would ask whether he was getting his medication and food. He reassured her that he was doing okay.

Zena contacted friends and community members and reached out to people who had previously helped families facing immigration detention.

His lawyers told the family that demonstrating community support could help at his bond hearing. Along with Zena, they organised a letter-writing event where people could write and notarise letters supporting Iemad.

For Zena, the response showed her that her family was not fighting alone.

"I don't think we expected to get over 150 letters of support," she said. "It was really amazing to see."

A wider ICE crackdown

Iemad's detention came as ICE has expanded its enforcement activity across the US.

ICE arrested 49,571 people in July, according to government data provided to the Deportation Data Project at the University of California Berkeley.

It was the highest monthly total of the second Trump administration, up 15 percent from June - and 70 percent from February.

'I don't think we expected to get over 150 letters to support. It was really amazing to see'

- Zena Saifo

The increase has also been accompanied by a growing number of arrests away from highly visible immigration raids, including arrests at workplaces, traffic stops and immigration appointments.

The result has been a growing sense of uncertainty among immigrants who might previously have regarded routine interactions with immigration authorities as relatively low-risk.

In July, more than half of those arrested had no criminal convictions or charges, according to the data.

The Trump administration and DHS have defended the crackdown as necessary to enforce US immigration law and have repeatedly said the agency was prioritising people with criminal records.

ICE defended Iemad's detention by pointing to his lack of permanent immigration status and his witness-tampering conviction.

"Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, ICE is targeting the worst of the worst," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement about Iemad.

"Nearly 70 percent of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the US."

'The fear doesn't just go away'

Iemad's release, however, has not erased the fear that he could be detained again.

His immigration case is still pending, and Zena said she remains worried about what could happen to her father and other immigrants facing the same system.

"The anxiety, the fear, the immense stress experienced the past two weeks, it's not just something that goes away," she said.

Now that Iemad is home, Zena said the family is grateful to the people who helped them through the ordeal.

But the experience has also changed how she sees the wider community around her.

Her father's detention, she said, showed that the consequences of an immigration crackdown can extend far beyond the person taken into custody, affecting families, friends and communities who are left to navigate the uncertainty with them.

"It really just shows we have a responsibility to the communities around us," she said. "We were able to ensure that we're standing up for others and that we don't let any harm go without being addressed."

text:
A man is calling for a criminal investigation after he said he was brutally attacked by ICE agents while walking to a bus stop in Arlington.

Jose Meijia Hernandez and his attorneys said he is taking matters into his own hand after going 17 days without help.

What we know:

Hernandez said he was walking to a bus stop on Columbia Pike to get to work when he was attacked. The incident left him with a brain injury.

The incident on Aug. 11 was captured on a cellphone video.

"Mr. Hernandez wakes up unconscious with blood all over his face, with his brain swelling because he suffered a brain injury," said his attorney Denisse Gastelum.

According to Hernandez, he was walking when he saw strangers approach who did not look like law enforcement. He got scared and started running, and later woke up bleeding all over his head and face.

Hernandez and his attorneys said they have not heard anything from local, state or federal law enforcement or lawmakers about how this was allowed to happen and what happens next.

On Friday, they filed a formal complaint with Arlington Police, asking them to launch a criminal investigation.

Arlington Commonwealth's Attorney Parisa Dehgani-Tafti says she supports diving deeper into the incident.

"It's absolutely necessary to send the message that nobody is above the law," Dehgani-Tafti said.

"Doesn't matter if you're a federal official or regular person on the street," she added. "Everybody must be held accountable, and I'll do my utmost to make sure that happens."

DHS refutes claims

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is refuting Hernandez's claims, saying he tried to flee and forced ICE agents to "use necessary force to gain control of the situation."

Hernandez was taken into custody and later to a hospital as a precaution, DHS officials said.

According to DHS, Hernandez entered the U.S. illegally from Mexico in 2006. He was arrested and accepted a voluntary return.

He returned at some point after 2008, officials said.

In 2020, DHS said Hernandez was convicted in Fairfax County for public intoxication. He was released from ICE custody with GPS monitoring. On Aug. 19, they removed an ankle monitor and began tracking Hernandez through his phone.

ICE agents said they provided fist aid to Hernandez and followed their training during the interaction.

In a statement, DHS said, "On August 11, 2026, ICE arrested Jose Mejia Hernandez, a criminal illegal alien from Mexico. During the arrest, he attempted the flee from the scene requiring ICE to use necessary force to gain control of the situation. He was taken into custody and later to a hospital out of precaution."

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement awarded a $16.7 million contract to a Kentucky-based firm on Thursday to buy electric gloves that can deliver painful shocks.

Why it matters: Some senators pushed back on the purchase, citing public scrutiny over the use of force by some ICE agents.

The CTG-5 Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, or G.L.O.V.E, is produced by Compliant Technologies, and their user guide says it should not be used against verbal defiance or as a form of punishment, Axios Avery Lotz writes.

The manufacturer advises against using it on the elderly, children, pregnant women and those with serious disabilities.

Zoom in: "ICE requires a non-lethal, de-escalation device intended to diffuse situations of high-stress environments where physical altercations are likely, such as field domestic disputes or inmate transport in jails," the contract paperwork filed by the Department of Homeland Security on Thursday reads.

"It will be used when a subject is actively or passively resisting and an officer needs to gain control quickly to prevent injuries to both parties."

According to a DHS notice published earlier this month, ICE officers must complete G.L.O.V.E. training and re-certification every two years.

Compliant Technologies did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

What they're saying: Sixteen senators sent ICE a letter Thursday expressing "deep concern" about the purchase and questioning the agency's "professional capability to safely deploy" the gloves.

The senators said that if ICE does acquire the gloves, it must publicly establish strict, enforceable limits on how they are deployed.

"A device capable of delivering an electrical shock through direct contact with an individual presents substantial risks if deployed during civil arrests – even more so if it is deployed without clear limits, appropriate training, and comprehensive oversight," they wrote.

The senators also said the acquisition "raises serious questions about necessity, proportionality, medical safety, training, accountability, and constitutional rights."

"Those questions are particularly important given the significant public scrutiny surrounding ICE's excessive use of force."

Between the lines: An analysis of 1,213 cases from January through December 2025 found that at least 375 incidents involved force or threatened force, according to the ACLU.

That includes 241 cases that involved physical force.

The other side: "Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from any safety equipment is despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers," a Homeland Security spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement.

"To be crystal clear: we will not abide by unconstitutional bans."

"Congressional Democrats have made it clear that they no longer support the brave men and women of ICE, and the inflammatory rhetoric they and their allies have levied against them has led to unprecedented levels of threats and assaults."

text:
An Edmonton-born man who lived most of his life in the United States is back in Canada, after losing a legal fight to remain south of the border to be with his two young sons.

Curtis Wright, 40, said he endured terrible conditions at different U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities in Texas after he was taken into custody 10 months ago.

Rather than self-deport to Canada, Wright said he fought to remain in the United States to raise the children he shares from a previous marriage.

"Can it be done from a different country? Sure, but that's going to be holidays and summers," Wright said in an interview from Kelowna, B.C.

"It drastically reduces my time and my ability to, you know, connect and be their father."

Wright said he was returned to Canada from the South Texas ICE Processing Centre a little more than two weeks ago. His sons, ages eight and 11, remain in Texas.

Wright moved to Houston in his youth. He later got work in the oil and gas industry.

In November, while coming back from a work trip in Mexico speaking with oil companies and distributors, he was interviewed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, and an old conviction resurfaced.

When he was 17, he said, he was convicted of drug possession and ordered to do community service and serve probation. Xanax, an anti-anxiety medication, had been found in his truck, he added.

Wright said that when he returned from Mexico, immigration agents shackled and hauled him away in the back of a van.

He spoke about U.S. President Donald Trump's heightened focus on deportation and noted his life in the country hadn't been an issue for nearly 30 years.

The whirlwind shift from unfettered freedom to being in federal custody was unbelievable, he said.

In the blaze of the Texas heat, he said, he ended up in freezing cold intake processing cells.

"The concrete that you're sitting on and laying on is colder than the air itself," he said.

Detainees were addressed by their dorm and bunk numbers rather than their names, he said, adding that the food was poor and the showers dirty and grimy.

"And some people would say that, 'Well, look where you are, maybe that's what you should expect.' And I say, well, we're still humans."

A spokesperson for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said the agency rejects the claim that people housed at the South Texas ICE Processing Centre "are being subjected to inhumane conditions or that the facility is operating under unsafe or overcrowded conditions."

"Individuals in ICE custody are provided appropriate meals and access to drinking water, hygiene facilities and recreation," Sarah Loicano said in an emailed statement.

She said ICE has no tolerance for abuse, discrimination or misconduct against people in custody.

Wright said he was ordered to be sent back to Canada in February on a removal order, but he appealed. He later learned from his lawyer that his appeal might take months more.

He said he decided to give up the fight in July and his removal order was finalized.

"I'd already been there for nine months and it was kind of time to just get out and go to Canada and kind of end this journey for everyone involved in my family," he said.

Wright said he considers himself lucky to be sent back to Canada rather than another country.

Some people he befriended in detention told him stories of fleeing oppressive governments. One said he had been detained days after his daughter was born and hadn't met her yet.

Immigration arrests in the United States dropped from January to May, but Trump's administration still plans to remove one million people this fiscal year, compared with roughly 442,000 people last year.

"I've been removed for a mistake I made 22 years ago, when I was a 17-year-old kid in high school. And now two American children are going to be left without their father," Wright said.

"I'm just one of thousands of others with similar stories.

"So when people talk about how this just affects immigrants, it's wrong. It affects many American families and children as well."

For now, Wright is staying at his parents' house in Kelowna with his fiancée, Kayla Thomsen, and their two-year-old daughter.

They plan to head to Edmonton so he can try to pick up a job with the same company he worked for in Texas.

Thomsen and the toddler travelled to B.C. to be with Wright when he arrived in Canada, first in Edmonton before moving west.

The first thing he did when he saw them was hug them, said Wright.

"That was No. 1."

SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- Immigration advocates say newly-released data shows a significant increase in immigration enforcement activity across the Bay Area and California.

The Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley released new figures after requesting and then suing the federal government for access to immigration enforcement data. According to the project, Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests in the San Francisco area increased nearly 70% compared with the same period a year earlier.

Data released by the project showed 2,928 ICE arrests from January through July 2025, compared with 4,970 arrests during the same period in 2026.

"We're at a rate of deportations that's at about five times where it was under the Biden administration," said David Hausman, co-director of the Deportation Data Project and an assistant professor of law at UC Berkeley.

MORE: ICE plans to purchase robot dogs

Hausman said the types of arrests being made have changed.

"Arresting people out in the community or at check-ins is really a new thing in the sense that it was really uncommon before this administration," Hausman said. "And now we're seeing much, much more of that. So, the rate of arrests not happening at jails or prisons has gone up by over ten times."

According to the data, ICE arrested 982 people in San Francisco in July, the highest monthly total since the project began releasing data. The project also reported 4,274 arrests statewide in California during the same month, which it described as record numbers.

Bill Hing, a University of San Francisco professor and director of the Immigration and Deportation Defense Clinic, said the figures reflect a broader enforcement presence across the region.

MORE: State Department preparing to cancel tens of thousands of visas held by asylum seekers: Officials

"These numbers tell us that ICE is here in the Bay Area, most people think that ICE is not only where there are sweeps and neighborhoods or Home Depot parking lots. But people should realize that every day ICE makes arrests all over the Bay Area," Hing said.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said, "ICE enforces the law as written. What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are illegally in the U.S. - full stop."

The department also said, "This data is being cherry picked by the Deportation Data Project to peddle a false narrative."

Asked about who is being detained during immigration appointments, Hing said some of those arrested have pending claims.

MORE: ICE plans to give officers gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks

"The people that are getting detained when we accompany our clients are people who have overstayed their visas, even if they have a legitimate asylum claim pending. So, no one is safe. This is not about people who are criminals," Hing said.

Data also shows that ICE has detained more than 600 children in California. In some cases, parents are being asked to bring passports and their children to immigration hearings.

"That's a clear sign that they're going to arrest the entire family, and they're going to deport them right away," Hing said.

The latest figures add to an ongoing debate over immigration enforcement practices in California and the Bay Area.

"Since Day One, DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump's promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists. We will continue to deliver on the President's promise to make America safe again.

"Our message is clear: if you come into our country illegally and break our laws, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you. ICE enforces the law as written. What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are illegally in the U.S.- full stop.

"This data is being cherry picked by the Deportation Data Project to peddle a false narrative.
