description:
Citizenship and Immigration Services and the U.S. Department of State issued two policies that place indefinite holds on green card applications and adjustment of diversity visa status.
Senior U.S. District Judge Edward Davila granted in part a preliminary injunction to temporarily reopen the processing of visa applications.
Generally, the Department of State selects up to 55,000 immigrants to start the application process for each fiscal year.
“Defendants highlight that … diversity visa adjudication requires extensive discretionary decisions made by thousands of consular officers and USCIS officials.
Citizenship and Immigration Services Joesph Edlow, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche as defendants.
text:
SAN JOSE, Calif. (CN) — A federal judge vacated three federal policies related to a stoppage approving immigration visas Friday, ruling they are considered final action by the government and have immediate consequences for noncitizens trying to apply for green cards.

In December 2025, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the U.S. Department of State issued two policies that place indefinite holds on green card applications and adjustment of diversity visa status.

And in February, the Department of State issued a notice pausing visa approval from 75 countries, requiring consular officers to refuse all immigrant visa applicants until the agency develops new guidance for consular officers to assess if an applicant might become dependent on public assistance once in the U.S. The notice was issued with no date on lifting the pause.

Senior U.S. District Judge Edward Davila granted in part a preliminary injunction to temporarily reopen the processing of visa applications. He also granted in part class certification of subclasses for those whose diversity visas, either under an Immigration Services or the Department of State policy, are currently on indefinite hold.

“Plaintiffs contend the three policies affect plaintiffs’ rights — by indefinitely pausing final adjudication, plaintiffs lose the opportunity to obtain lawful permanent residency and all the benefits that accompany it, i.e., the ability to live, work, and study in the United States. And the possibility that the policies may be revised in the future does not defeat finality,” the Barack Obama appointee wrote in his 23-page ruling.

“The court agrees with plaintiffs’ characterization of the policies. Despite their temporary characterizations, there is no indication when, or if, they will be lifted or modified, and in the interim, the policies have upended the normal diversity visa processing procedures and had immediate legal consequences on plaintiffs,” he wrote.

Under the diversity immigrant visa program, the Department of State holds a lottery in which it randomly selects noncitizens from countries with historically low rates of U.S. immigration for the opportunity to apply for a green card. If an applicant is in the U.S. under a different visa at the time of selection, they must a submit form with Immigration Services to adjust their status to permanent resident.

Selection to the program does not guarantee a visa, just the ability to apply for one. Generally, the Department of State selects up to 55,000 immigrants to start the application process for each fiscal year.

Davila was not convinced by the government’s arguments that the policies did not indicate final agency action, a necessary step to grant a preliminary injunction.

“The characterization of the policies as ‘temporary’ does not exempt them from judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act,” he wrote.

Davila also wasn’t persuaded by the government’s arguments that processing the visas currently in limbo would be a bureaucratic nightmare.

“Defendants highlight that … diversity visa adjudication requires extensive discretionary decisions made by thousands of consular officers and USCIS officials. This is true. Rather than challenging the determination of any one application — an area in which the court likely lacks jurisdiction in any event — plaintiffs challenge the agencies’ categorical decisions to cease adjudication and/or approval of the applications all together,” wrote Davila.

“Defendants’ argument that it would be difficult for them to comply with any order requiring adjudication within a certain time period, or that there are individual issues with certain class members that may prevent them from actually having their applications adjudicated, is irrelevant.”

The class action was filed in June in Northern California federal court and names President Donald Trump, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Director of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Joesph Edlow, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche as defendants.

Attorneys representing the class and federal officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

text:
FIRE challenged the two statutes the administration weaponized to try and deport Mahmoud Khalil and Rümeysa Öztürk

Decision is the first in the country to squarely rule on the constitutionality of these statutes and thus will reverberate in similar proceedings around the country

Judge: ‘Stated plainly, in the United States, freedom of speech belongs to the people. It is not the government’s to take.’

SAN JOSE, Calif., Aug. 28, 2026 — Today, a federal court ruled that the provisions Secretary of State Marco Rubio used in an attempt to deport legal immigrants for their speech are unconstitutional and violate the First Amendment.

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression challenged the provisions in August 2025. The ruling affirms a bedrock constitutional principle: The government cannot punish people for protected speech simply because officials dislike their views.

“In America, free speech doesn’t just belong to the people who say things the government agrees with,” said FIRE attorney Conor Fitzpatrick. “Today’s ruling proves that free speech isn’t a privilege, but the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child.”

Judge Noël Wise of the United States District Court for the Northern District of California wrote in her opinion that “in the United States, freedom of speech belongs to the people. It is not the government’s to take.”

“Foundational to America’s enduring democracy are our freedoms of speech and the press embodied in the First Amendment,” she wrote. “In the United States, free speech, including the freedom to criticize the government and its leaders, is not a sign of our democracy’s fragility. It is evidence of its strength. That strength is diminished when members of our society — citizens and noncitizens alike — must self-censor and ‘behave’ or suffer the government’s retaliation.”

Rubio and the Trump administration sought to use immigration law to target foreign university students and others for deportation based on protected speech like writing op-eds and attending protests. Their attack suppressed the speech of noncitizens, who worried that voicing the “wrong” opinion about America or Israel will result in deportation. Today’s decision means that the noncitizen writers and editors of Stanford Daily, and Jane Doe, may not have their visas revoked or be deported based on protected speech. And it is the first ruling in the country to squarely rule on the constitutionality of these statutes and thus will reverberate in similar proceedings around the country, including those of Mahmoud Khalil and Moshen Mahdawi.

Noncitizens in the United States have First Amendment rights. Despite that, Rubio used two provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act to target lawfully present noncitizens for their opinions.

The first allows the secretary of state to initiate deportation proceedings against any noncitizen for protected speech if the secretary “personally determines” the speech “compromises a compelling foreign policy interest.”

The second enables the secretary of state to revoke the visa of any noncitizen “at any time” for any reason.

FIRE argued that the provisions are unconstitutional when used to revoke a visa or deport someone for speech the First Amendment protects. Today, the court agreed.

Rubio used the first provision to target Columbia University students Mahmoud Khalil and Moshen Mahdawi for protected pro-Palestinian speech and the second to target Tufts University student Rümeysa Öztürk for coauthoring an op-ed.

Rubio and the Trump administration claimed that this political speech comes from noncitizens, which therefore warrants setting aside America's protection of free speech. That’s wrong.

America’s founding principle is that liberty comes not from the government, but is an inherent right of every individual. Every person — whether they’re a U.S. citizen, are visiting for the week, or are here on a student visa — has free speech rights in this country.

Plaintiffs in FIRE’s lawsuit represented the wide range of groups and individuals whose speech is threatened by the continued assault on noncitizens’ protected speech:

The Stanford Daily, the independent, student-run newspaper at Stanford University, where writers with student visas are declining assignments related to the conflict in the Middle East, worried that even reporting on the war will endanger their immigration status

Jane Doe, a legal noncitizen with no criminal record who engaged in pro-Palestinian speech and fears deportation and visa revocation because of her expression

“The reporters in our newsroom shouldn’t have to fear that writing a story will result in their deportation,” said George Porteous, editor-in-chief of The Stanford Daily. “Today’s victory means they won’t have to. The Court’s decision will enable our reporters to focus on what they do best: asking tough questions and reporting the truth.”

FIRE aimed to stop the government’s use of the two provisions that stand counter to our ideals as a nation: Provisions that — in their expansive scope and unchecked authority — are more at home in countries like China and Russia than in a free America.

Marc Van Der Hout, Johnny Sinodis, and Oona Cahill at Van Der Hout LLP served as local and advisory counsel on the case.

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization dedicated to defending and sustaining the individual rights of all Americans to free speech and free thought — the most essential qualities of liberty.

text:
Washington is among four states being sued by the Trump administration over in-state college tuition for immigrant students.

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed lawsuits Thursday against Washington, Oregon, Arizona, and New Mexico, arguing their laws illegally give some immigrants tuition benefits that aren’t available to all U.S. citizens, according to a news release from the DOJ. The lawsuits bring the DOJ’s total to 21 states sued over the issue.

“Over 30 years ago, Congress made clear that States cannot put illegal aliens before our Nation’s own citizens,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. stated. “By granting illegal aliens in-state tuition, Washington, Oregon, New Mexico, and Arizona are pushing citizens to the side and ignoring federal law.”

The DOJ is seeking court orders to block the four states from enforcing laws that require colleges and universities to provide in-state tuition rates to all residents regardless of immigration status, as well as state laws providing financial assistance and scholarships to undocumented immigrants.

“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division stated. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.”

WA attorney general vows to defend immigrant students

The DOJ is asking courts to block those laws, but the Washington State Attorney General’s (AG) Office is pushing back.

“The administration is challenging longstanding Washington laws that recognize the potential of all our residents regardless of citizenship status,” a spokesperson for the AG’s Office stated. “We look forward to defending Washington law against this politically motivated lawsuit.”

According to the DOJ, the department has won similar lawsuits in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska and Illinois. Those cases resulted in court orders permanently blocking similar state tuition laws. Lawsuits are also pending in 12 other states, including California, New York, New Jersey, Minnesota, Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Maryland and Kansas.

Contributing: Katrina Guischard, KIRO Newsradio; Julia Dallas, MyNorthwest

title: Caribbean immigration advocates praise lawsuit against Rensselaer sheriff for violating law ...
description:
Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault has refused to terminate its 287(g) agreement.
“Every law enforcement agency in New York has a duty to serve and protect every resident, while upholding state and local law,” Awawdeh said.
“Instead of complying with the new state law, the Sheriff’s Office in Rensselaer County has chosen to defy state law, putting political posturing ahead of its responsibilities and obligations to its community.
“All law enforcement agencies are expected to uphold New York’s laws,” said Attorney General James.
The state alleges that the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office has failed to perform duties required of it under state law.
text:
The legislation prohibits New York State and local law enforcement agencies and local governments from entering into or maintaining 287(g) agreements with ICE for federal civil immigration enforcement and requires any agreements in place to be terminated by Aug. 25, 2026.

Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault has refused to terminate its 287(g) agreement.

“We applaud Attorney General Letitia James and Governor Hochul for taking every step necessary to ensure that New York’s law enforcement agencies remain accountable to the communities they serve and focused on keeping all New Yorkers safe, not carrying out ICE and the Trump administration’s deportation agenda,” Murad Awawdeh, president and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition (NYIC), told Caribbean Life on Thursday.

NYIC is an umbrella organization of over 200 immigrant and refugee groups in New York State.

“Every law enforcement agency in New York has a duty to serve and protect every resident, while upholding state and local law,” Awawdeh said. “Instead of complying with the new state law, the Sheriff’s Office in Rensselaer County has chosen to defy state law, putting political posturing ahead of its responsibilities and obligations to its community.

“This lawsuit makes clear that no one is above the law, not even an elected sheriff,” he continued.

Earlier on Thursday, James and Hochul announced the lawsuit against the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office for failing to comply with New York’s Local Cops, Local Crimes Act (LCLCA).

“All law enforcement agencies are expected to uphold New York’s laws,” said Attorney General James. “The Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office has been given every opportunity to follow the law, yet has chosen not to.

“My office is suing to enforce New York’s laws and ensure that local law enforcement agencies remain focused on their most fundamental responsibility: keeping New Yorkers safe,” she added.

Governor Hochul said: “Compliance with the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act is not optional. Rensselaer County’s failure to act in accordance with the law sends a clear message: these elected leaders are not serious about New Yorkers’ safety.

“Today, we are taking action to ensure the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office performs the duties required of it under state law, because no one in New York State is above the law,” she added.

James said section 287(g) agreements are agreements between ICE and state or local law enforcement agencies that allow local officers to perform certain federal civil immigration enforcement functions. Depending on the agreement, she said local officers can be authorized to question, arrest and detain Caribbean and other immigrants for suspected violations of federal civil immigration law.

The New York Attorney General said LCLCA, signed into law by Hochul on May 27, 2026, prohibits local law enforcement agencies from entering or remaining in these agreements with the federal government.

She said the law required agencies that already had these agreements to exercise their termination provisions within 90 days, by Aug. 25, 2026.

“Any covered agreement still in effect on that date is deemed void and unenforceable under state law,” said James, stating that the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office has maintained a 287(g) agreement with ICE since March 2020.

After the LCLCA was enacted, she said the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) notified the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office of the new law and requested information regarding the status of the agency’s 287(g) agreement.

James said the OAG did not receive a response confirming that the agreement had been terminated or would be terminated by the Aug. 25 deadline.

On Aug. 19, she said OAG issued a formal investigative demand pursuant to New York Executive Law Section 63-E, or subpoena, seeking documents sufficient to show what actions the agency had taken to terminate its 287(g) agreement.

The New York attorney general said OAG still has not received confirmation that the agreement has been terminated.

“Meanwhile, officials in Rensselaer County have made public statements indicating their intent to defy the law, with one telling a reporter that OAG and the Governor’s Office ‘could take that letter, crumple it up and shove it,’” James said.

She said that, of the 12 law enforcement agencies that had 287(g) agreements before the LCLCA took effect, the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office is the only one that has not indicated its intent to dissolve its agreement.

The state alleges that the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office has failed to perform duties required of it under state law.

James said the suit requests that the Rensselaer County Supreme Court order the Sheriff’s Office to exercise the termination provisions in its 287(g) agreement and to declare the agreement void and unenforceable under New York law.

She said Thursday’s lawsuit is the first legal action brought by the OAG’s newly established Office of Immigrant Trust (OIT) under the LCLCA.

James said the OIT was created to enforce New York laws limiting state and local involvement in federal civil immigration enforcement, and is authorized to investigate potential violations and bring civil actions when warranted.

She said that, in June, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a federal lawsuit challenging the LCLCA.

But, on Aug. 3, the US District Court for the Northern District of New York denied the federal government’s request to block New York’s ban on 287(g) agreements, allowing the state’s Aug. 25 deadline to unwind these agreements to remain in effect.

Following an unprecedented escalation in aggressive Trump administration immigration enforcement, Hochul said she has been fighting to protect New Yorkers from federal actions that “indiscriminately target” Caribbean and other immigrant communities.

Earlier this year, she signed what she characterized as “one of the most comprehensive laws in the nation to rein in ICE and prevent Trump’s overreach” by prohibiting local governments, state and local police, and state and local corrections from entering into 287(g) Agreements or similar agreements with the federal government that allow for state and local law enforcement personnel and facilities to be used for civil immigration enforcement purposes.

The laws also prohibit state, local, and federal officers from wearing face covering while interacting with the public.

In addition, among other things, the governor established a state law under which New Yorkers can bring a lawsuit against federal, state and local government officials for a violation of their constitutional rights, and keep immigration authorities out of sensitive locations.

text:
For daily news, updates, and analysis, be sure to follow us on Instagram. If you are able to support independent journalism, please make a tax-deductible donation to News Not Noise here.

The Trump administration is taking people — from their homes, workplaces, courthouses, and the streets — on an extraordinary scale. They’re holding many of them for months before deporting them. Some are sent to countries they don’t know. Some are U.S. citizens. Some are dying in custody.

The Trump administration calls this mass deportation and says it’s “improving Americans’ quality of life.” A growing majority of Americans disagree.

Because the program is unfolding in individual raids, across hundreds of courtrooms, private prisons, and government flights, it’s hard to see the big picture. Today we’re pulling back from the daily torrent to show you what this campaign adds up to: Who is being taken, what happens to them, what this campaign costs, and what it is doing to the country.

News Not Noise Explains: Mass Deportation

How Many People? The U.S. government says it deported more than 675,000 people in 2025. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claims 2.2 million more left the country voluntarily, which the administration calls “self-deportation.” There’s reason to doubt that number. An analysis by the Center for Migration Studies concluded the true figure is closer to one-tenth of that. As of July, about 132,000 people had left the U.S. through DHS’s billion-dollar “self-deportation” program, called Project Homecoming, and another 70,000 were signed up to leave. (The contract went to a firm that had never served as a lead government contractor and is run by a MAGA businessman. DHS itself concluded the contract award had the “appearance of impropriety.”)

What Do Numbers Mean, Anyway? To understand the scale, it helps to know how many undocumented immigrants live in the U.S. Trump claims there are more than 25 million, while his allies offer even more exaggerated figures. There are likely a little over 15 million, down from a peak of 15.8 million in mid-2024, according to the latest estimate by the Migration Policy Institute.

Who’s Targeted: Trump and his allies have repeatedly insisted they are targeting criminals, “the worst of the worst.” They also use dehumanizing language about immigrants. “They’re not humans,” Trump has said. “They’re animals.” Historically, ICE prioritized arresting people with criminal records. The Trump administration changed that. Arrests of non-citizens without criminal convictions are up 8.7-fold. People with no criminal record now make up over 70% of detainees.

Share

Citizens: More than 170 U.S. citizens have been detained by immigration agents, according to a ProPublica investigation. Citizens have been beaten, tased, and shot by immigration agents, many at peaceful anti-ICE protests; two have been killed. ICE’s use of crowd control weapons, like tear gas and rubber bullets, has led to blindings and traumatic brain injuries. An ACLU investigation found that hundreds of journalists, elected officials, community observers, and children, many of them U.S. citizens, were detained, targeted, or “subjected to law enforcement misconduct” in 2025.

Children: The Marshall Project found that the Trump administration has detained thousands of children, roughly ten times as many as the Biden administration. Asked about detaining kids, an ICE spokesperson told the Marshall Project that “being in detention is a choice,” a phrase the agency has repeatedly used.

Share

From the Border to Your Door: The administration shifted immigration enforcement away from the border and deeper into the country, while pushing agents to meet unprecedented arrest quotas. It has reassigned tens of thousands of federal agents from other agencies to immigration cases. That includes 80% of special agents at the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, resulting in fewer investigations of drug and gun crimes. It also includes 23% of FBI agents — up to 40% in some large offices — who might otherwise be investigating crimes like terrorism. Thanks to the Supreme Court, immigration agents have also been given broader latitude to use race, language, and occupation when deciding whom to stop or question. DHS claimed in an internal memo that its agents could enter homes without a judicial warrant, contradicting decades of legal precedent and potentially the Constitution.

Detention: The U.S. is setting records for the number of people held in immigration detention. Republicans in Congress handed ICE $45 billion to detain immigrants through Trump’s second term; that’s more than the last three administrations spent on detention, combined. The Trump administration has pushed a “mandatory detention” policy. For decades, detention was generally reserved for people considered dangerous or likely to flee. Others were often released on bond while their cases moved through the courts. Under Trump, ICE reversed that policy. Now the vast majority of those taken are held until they receive a final deportation decision, which can mean months locked up, often for people with no criminal record. Advocates argue this makes the process so difficult that people give up, and intimidates others who fear they could be next. More than 400 judges across the country, nominated by every president since Reagan, have ruled against “mandatory detention,” and the Supreme Court will consider the issue later this year.

description:

Yiannopoulos previously said he was gay but in recent years has said he no longer identifies as such.
text:
Controversial British figure Milo Yiannopoulos, who gained a reputation as a right-wing provocateur more than a decade ago, has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Department of Homeland Security said Friday.

Yiannopoulos was arrested on Thursday at a Louisiana airport, DHS said. He was still in custody as of Friday afternoon, according to the agency’s online detainee locator.

Yiannopoulos legally entered the country in 2019, but “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws,” DHS added.

“Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing,” the agency said in a post on X. “He will remain in ICE custody pending removal.”

Yiannopoulos is known as a conservative firebrand. Among other public statements and appearances, he attracted considerable public attention after embarking on a bus tour of US college campuses he branded the “Dangerous F*ggot” bus tour, which he said was intended to promote free speech and bring his perspective to universities where he believed liberal ideas may dominate the campus conversation. His disparaging remarks about Muslims, transgender people and others drew outrage from many who argued the racist and hateful language was an attempt to stoke tensions on campus and should not be platformed by colleges and universities.

His appearances on some campuses drew loud protests. While many demonstrations were peaceful, Yiannopoulos’ visit to University of California, Berkeley in February 2017 resulted in the event being canceled after a large protest became violent and destructive and two Republican students were attacked, the university said at the time.

Yiannopoulos has voiced support of immigration enforcement as recently as last year. In a post on X, he called for ICE checkpoints in California supermarkets and other common areas and “on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally.”

Far right influencer Laura Loomer, who has feuded with Yiannopoulos, said in a post on X Friday that she had reported him to ICE and the FBI.

His rise to prominence coincided with Donald Trump’s ascent in national politics and the president’s entry to the White House. Yiannopoulos had positioned himself as one of the president’s avid supporters, sometimes referring to Trump as “Daddy.”

In an interview with CNN in 2017, he connected the support he was receiving with the conservative movement that drove Trump’s successful campaign.

“People are tired of being told how to live, how to speak, what language they can use,” he said. “The strength of feeling in my crowds, the enthusiasm for me from the audiences is the same – the same instinct, the same sort of motivating force (that) put Trump in the White House.”

Though Yiannopoulos, who was born in England and worked for several years as an editor for Breitbart News, found footholds for his ideas among some conservative groups and college students in the US, he has seen his profile dwindle.

In 2016, Yiannopoulos was permanently banned from Twitter, now known as X. He was seen as an instigator of online attacks on Leslie Jones, the former Saturday Night Live comedian. Yiannopoulos’ account was eventually reinstated after Elon Musk bought the social media platform, and he had posted as recently as Thursday evening.

He came under intense scrutiny in 2017 after his comments appeared to condone pedophilia. He then resigned from Breitbart amid backlash to his comments, offering a rare apology though said his comments were deceptively edited.

Yiannopoulos previously said he was gay but in recent years has said he no longer identifies as such. He told Tucker Carlson last year, “mainstreaming homosexuality in the Republican Party is the great regret of my life.”

Yiannopoulos’ Telegram, which hasn’t had posts since at least January 2025, said he was opening a clinic in Florida that would help “men plagued by same-sex attraction.” Yiannopoulos also identified himself as a “retired civil rights icon.”

In June 2022, Yiannopoulos said in a Telegram post that he was an unpaid intern to former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, a lighting rod Republican from Georgia.

Yiannopoulos also worked on the 2024 presidential campaign of Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West who fell from grace after a series of antisemitic comments. Yiannopoulos was also Ye’s chief of staff to the rapper.

This story has been updated with additional information.

description:
In February, the board authorized the England Airpark Executive Director to sign contracts with the federal government to move forward on the detention center.
The room holding the Thursday board meeting was packed.
There were two items up for discussion that drew particular scrutiny from members of the public who addressed the board.
He said that Hennessy knows that it was the local board that decided to sign the contracts with the federal government.
“More importantly the people of Alexandria know that, and the people of Louisiana know that,” González said.
text:
The fight over a Trump administration plan to detain immigrant families and children at the site of a former military base in Alexandria heated up Thursday (Aug. 27), as residents of central Louisiana and immigrant rights advocates from across the state showed up at a local board meeting to voice their opposition to the proposed detention facility.

Despite public condemnation of the two agenda items pertaining to immigration enforcement and increased procedural hurdles to public gatherings on the former base, the 10-member England Authority Board of Commissioners — which governs the England Airpark, the proposed location of the facility — passed both items.

But the board acknowledged mounting public concerns over family and children detention at the airpark, a former base that is also home to the Alexandria International Airport, and announced a follow-up meeting set for Sept. 8 to address the issue.

Residents and immigrant rights advocates characterized the announcement as a victory for a months-long effort to publicly address the board regarding their concerns about using the airpark to house families and children at the Louisiana facility.

“Hopefully with them opening up this Sept. 8 special meeting to talk about the detention center for women and children, that will give us room to actually express those views, and that they can hear those views, because they didn’t want to hear them today,” said DC Sills, an Alexandria-based minister, who spoke with Verite News after the meeting.

In February, the board authorized the England Airpark Executive Director to sign contracts with the federal government to move forward on the detention center. Those contracts have since been signed. As planned, the facility will house 500 migrant families and unaccompanied children, with convenient access to the Alexandria airport, which is a major hub for deportation flights in the United States.

The room holding the Thursday board meeting was packed. Two busloads of people opposed to the project — one traveling from Lafayette, the others from New Orleans and Baton Rouge — joined locals cramming themselves into the boardroom spilling out into the hallway and into two overflow rooms to voice their opposition to immigration operations there and listen in to the meeting.

Mich González, an attorney with the Southern Poverty Law Center who rode to Alexandria with a group from New Orleans, said that the growing number of people attending these meetings to voice opposition reflects the concern from Alexandria residents and people across Louisiana who don’t want to have a family and child detention center in the state and who don’t trust U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“It’s hard for people to get there,” he said about Alexandria. “But I guarantee you, as this continues to pick up, and the public becomes more and more aware of what’s going on, that number will just keep growing.”

Conrad Cable, a Democratic candidate running for the U.S. House of Representatives in Louisiana’s 4th Congressional District — which covers much of the western portion of the state — was also among the group that traveled to Alexandria. Cable said that although the airpark is not in the district that he’s trying to win, the human rights implications of having people incarcerated in a facility like the one being built in Alexandria prompted him to come and lend his support to those in attendance.

“I’m here today to advocate for there to be a reform in this country to the immigration process that allows for people, through funding our courts and having more immigration judges, to see these asylum seekers and to make immigration in this country a reality for people who are trying to live their version of the American dream,” Cable told Verite News.

Local activists praised the fact that people from outside of the city came to show their support for the Rapides Parish residents who oppose the facility.

“I’m just so grateful for the turnout and all of this attention and pressure that we’re putting on the board, especially because they were not previously listening to this community,” said Erin Tracy, a Pineville-based activist, who said she reached out to statewide groups to help draw attention to the issue.

“We did have to bring in outside help to show them that the whole state is watching you and this country is about to be watching you,” Tracy said.

There were two items up for discussion that drew particular scrutiny from members of the public who addressed the board. One was a motion to authorize England Airpark Executive Director Ralph Hennessy to sign a lease agreement with CSI Aviation, a transportation and air charter company that has had multi-million-dollar contracts with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and ICE for transport and removal operations. The agreement would allow CSI Aviation to move from a temporary office space on the airfield to a permanent structure that had been recently vacated. The second was a new policy requiring permits for protests at the airpark.

In an interview with Verite News, Hennessy characterized the agreement with CSI Aviation as having minimal impact, saying that had the board not agreed to approve the lease, the company would have just continued to operate out of the temporary space. But some residents depicted the agreement as morally wrong.

“Blood money taken from CSI Aviation. Money soaked in pain, agony and tears, and yes spilt blood is not a public good,” Patrick McGinty, a resident of Alexandria, said in a public comment to the board.

McGinty was one of several speakers that criticized the agreement with the transport company.

David Broussard, the deputy director of the airpark, said during the board meeting that the new building would fit CSI Aviation’s operational needs perfectly, and that the company is going to ramp up and hire an additional 100 employees. Broussard did not specify when the hiring would happen.

CSI Aviation did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

When it came to regulations around public demonstrations, England Airpark said, in an open letter to the public, that the regulations it was seeking to implement were “intended to balance First Amendment rights with the safe and orderly use of public property, not to suppress any particular viewpoint or cause.”

But opponents of the proposed policy expressed concern and confusion around the 19-page regulation, depicting it as an attempt to stifle the right to assemble.

“There’s going to be a permitting process to provide for spontaneous demonstrations. How do you get a permit for something that’s spontaneous?” asked Dena Norton, a Pineville resident who came to the meeting with her sister, Rose Marie Norton, to address her concerns about what she said were potential hindrances to their First Amendment rights.

Dena Norton criticized the document as difficult for the community to understand, adding that it lacked clarity surrounding how long it takes to get a permit and included permitting fees, which she said goes against the ability of the public to express its opinion on an issue.

“It sounds more like you’re trying to prohibit people or place obstacles for them to do what is our constitutional right,” she told the board.

The board discussed and agreed to remove language that would require protestors to secure insurance coverage for any planned demonstration, saying the requirement was overly burdensome. But board members passed the measure with the permit requirements still in place.

“The concern about insurance, I wonder how much insurance the Tea Party group had in Boston that brought in the revolution,” said Kristina Peterson, a resident of Sabine Parish.

Peterson said that one of her main concerns that drove her to show up on Thursday was what she saw as an attack on protesters’ First Amendment rights. She said she’s worried that incremental efforts to diminish those rights creates fertile ground for an easy slip into authoritarianism.

When asked to comment on Thursday’s meeting, Hennessy said he wasn’t sure what the point of the Sept. 8 meeting would be, given that the contracts authorizing the detention center had already been signed.

He also said that the focus on local level authorities was misplaced.

“If people are unhappy with those policies, take them up in Washington, D.C., not here, because you’re not going to change it here,” Hennessy said.

González, however, said that he thinks local level action is important and appropriate. He said that Hennessy knows that it was the local board that decided to sign the contracts with the federal government.

“More importantly the people of Alexandria know that, and the people of Louisiana know that,” González said. “We look forward to reminding him of that when we see him on Sept. 8.”

Bobbi-Jeanne Misick contributed to this report.

What's next?

The 41-year-old British national, a strong supporter of Donald Trump's harsh immigration policies, is now awaiting deportation.

British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos, who was banned from entering Australia in 2019 over his anti-Islam commentary, has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Mr Yiannopoulos, 41, was arrested on Thursday at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport.

His arrest comes after he called for ICE checkpoints at supermarkets in the United States, with summary deportation of anyone failing to prove legal US residency.

The US Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, said in a statement that he was subject to a final order of removal from the US, describing him as "an illegal alien from the United Kingdom".

According to DHS, Mr Yiannopoulos legally entered the US in May 2019 through New York City but "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws".

"Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on July 22 after failing to show up for his immigration hearing," the DHS statement said.

" He will remain in ICE custody pending removal. "

Mr Yiannopoulos was not immediately available for comment and it was unclear whether he had obtained legal representation.

Celebrity news site TMZ.com broke the news of his arrest and suggested Mr Yiannopoulos was in New Orleans ahead of a scheduled performance by the artist formerly known as Kanye West on Friday night.

Mr Yiannopoulos has close ties to the hip-hop star.

ICE's detention of Mr Yiannopoulos marked an ironic turn for the political pundit who is known for far-right-wing commentary.

It includes anti-Islamic rhetoric and support for immigration enforcement beyond the crackdown instituted by US President Donald Trump.

In a June 2025 post on the social media platform X he said California "needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they are in the US legally".

In addition to his association with West, Mr Yiannopoulos has collaborated with white nationalist Nick Fuentes.

He started working for right-wing Breitbart News in 2014 where he gained notoriety for his prominent role in the "Gamergate" anti-feminist harassment campaign that targeted women in the video game industry.

text:
Washington, D.C. – In case you missed it, U.S. Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla (both D-Calif.) joined Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) and Senate colleagues to call on the Trump Administration to abandon its reckless plan to outfit U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers with gloves that deliver painful electric shocks. Their letter also demands that ICE provide Congress with answers and documentation for over 30 questions about how these devices will be used, the protocol for using them, safety guardrails, accountability measures, and more.

On August 10, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a notice concerning ICE’s planned acquisition of the CTG-5 G.L.O.V.E., a glove designed to deliver a painful electric shock. The notice estimates the potential value of the acquisition between $10 million and $20 million. Despite opposition, on August 27, ICE moved forward with a $16.7 million no-bid contract for these gloves without providing Congress responses to questions.

“We write to express deep concern about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to spend up to $20 million on gloves that deliver electric shocks,” the Senators began. “…The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant skepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause. Therefore, we urge ICE to cancel the contract and reconsider the purchase.”

“The proposed acquisition raises serious questions about necessity, proportionality, medical safety, training, accountability, and constitutional rights,” the Senators continued. “Those questions are particularly important given the significant public scrutiny surrounding ICE’s excessive use of force. A device capable of delivering an electrical shock through direct contact with an individual presents substantial risks if deployed during civil arrests – even more so if it is deployed without clear limits, appropriate training, and comprehensive oversight.”

“At a time when the American people have demanded de-escalation in immigration enforcement, it is not clear why existing tools and tactics are insufficient for the agency,” the Senators wrote. “In the past year, DHS has repeatedly spent millions of taxpayer dollars on purchases it ends up not using, including $464 million for airplanes, $700 million on warehouses, and more than $2.25 million for SUVs wrapped with ICE branding. Many of these ICE transactions, including the planned electric-shock glove purchase, are completed through no-bid contracts that circumvent the normal competitive procurement process without a sufficient rationale.”

“If ICE proceeds with purchasing $20 million worth of electric-shock gloves, Congress needs a clear understanding of the device’s safety and authorized uses,” the Senators concluded.

The letter was also signed by Senators Angus King (I-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.).

The full text of the letter can be viewed here and below.

Dear Acting Director Venturella,

We write to express deep concern about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to spend up to $20 million on gloves that deliver electric shocks. Over the past year, ICE personnel have been involved in numerous well-documented incidents of excessive force and civil rights violations. These incidents have shown the American people that ICE personnel are not adequately trained or accountable for their interactions with civilians. The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant skepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause. Therefore, we urge ICE to cancel the contract and reconsider the purchase.

On August 10, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a notice concerning ICE’s planned acquisition of the CTG-5 G.L.O.V.E., a glove designed to deliver a painful electric shock that is described as a “Conductive Distraction and De-escalation Device,” for use by both Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO). The notice estimates the potential value of the acquisition between $10 million and $20 million. Congress has an obligation to ensure that federal law enforcement agencies have the resources necessary to perform their duties safely and effectively while ensuring that taxpayer dollars are being used for tools that are necessary, proportionate, and subject to meaningful safeguards. The proposed acquisition raises serious questions about necessity, proportionality, medical safety, training, accountability, and constitutional rights. Those questions are particularly important given the significant public scrutiny surrounding ICE’s excessive use of force. A device capable of delivering an electrical shock through direct contact with an individual presents substantial risks if deployed during civil arrests – even more so if it is deployed without clear limits, appropriate training, and comprehensive oversight.

ICE personnel have access to pepper spray, Tasers, batons, and restraint techniques, not to mention deescalation strategies that are widely used by law enforcement throughout the country. At a time when the American people have demanded de-escalation in immigration enforcement, it is not clear why existing tools and tactics are insufficient for the agency. In the past year, DHS has repeatedly spent millions of taxpayer dollars on purchases it ends up not using, including $464 million for airplanes, $700 million on warehouses, and more than $2.25 million for SUVs wrapped with ICE branding. Many of these ICE transactions, including the planned electric shock glove purchase, are completed through no-bid contracts that circumvent the normal competitive procurement process without a sufficient rationale. This history raises concerns about wasteful spending and unethical contracting practices that could benefit individuals who have personal relationships with administration officials rather than those who can provide the best service at the lowest cost to the taxpayer.

If ICE proceeds with purchasing $20 million worth of electric-shock gloves, Congress needs a clear understanding of the device’s safety and authorized uses. The manufacturer identifies restrictions on the device’s use, including limitations involving children, pregnant women, elderly or disabled individuals, and repeated or simultaneous use. The manufacturer also warns that use of the electric-shock glove may cause or contribute to death or serious injury, and that longer exposure increases that potential risk. If it proceeds with this contract, ICE must establish and make public clear, enforceable limits on when and against whom the electric-shock gloves may be used, especially given that ICE may not be able to immediately assess whether an individual is pregnant or disabled. Given that ICE is most frequently engaged in civil immigration enforcement rather than criminal arrests, the agency must carefully evaluate whether deployment of the electric-shock gloves in such situations is proportionate to the task.

ICE must also establish and make public the training requirements the agency will put in place prior to and throughout any potential deployment of these gloves. Over the past year, ICE has undermined the public’s trust in the agency’s training standards by putting new personnel into operational situations who are not properly vetted or adequately trained. Training for ICE recruits was slashed before being extended again following significant backlash. Additionally, ICE has put new recruits in the field before even completing their background checks, with tragic consequences. The issuance of these electric-shock gloves to personnel in the field without sufficient training would be yet another failure of ICE in the eyes of the public.

ICE has continually failed to meet basic standards of transparency and accountability. The electric-shock gloves present a particular accountability challenge because the use of force may cause significant pain and internal injury without necessarily producing obvious visible injuries. If the electric-shock gloves are deployed, ICE must establish a robust system for documenting and reviewing every deployment and instance of use. ICE should not deploy the gloves without evidence that personnel understand and take seriously the device’s risks and that individuals subjected to its use can receive an appropriate medical response. ICE must also ensure robust internal procedures for investigating misuse of the device and all use-of-force tools provided to personnel, and effective consequences for those who are found to have abused them.

In light of these many concerns, we request answers to the following questions and production of the documents identified below.

Necessity, Procurement, and Alternatives

What specific operational capability does the G.L.O.V.E. provide that existing ICE defensive tactics and less-lethal tools—including pepper spray, Tasers, batons, and restraint techniques—do not? Please provide the operational analysis or other documentation supporting the acquisition.

How many electric-shock gloves does ICE intend to purchase, at what projected per-unit cost? How many personnel will be issued the device?

What alternatives did ICE consider before selecting the G.L.O.V.E.?

Did ICE consult with other law enforcement agencies that use the device regarding effectiveness, injuries, complaints, misuse, training requirements, or other concerns?

Please provide the justification for the purchase of the G.L.O.V.E. via a non-competitive contract process.

Safety and Appropriate Use

How does ICE classify the G.L.O.V.E. under DHS Use of Force Policy 044-05? Are the electric-shock gloves considered a de-escalation tactic under this policy?

In what specific circumstances will use of the electric-shock gloves be authorized?

Will use of the electric-shock gloves require supervisory authorization?

Which positions and units will carry the device?

What is the protocol for usage of the electric-shock gloves? Will ICE personnel be instructed to issue a warning before gloves are activated?

Will ICE expressly prohibit use of the electric-shock gloves as a routine compliance or punishment tool?

What restrictions will apply to vulnerable populations?

Will ICE prohibit the use of the electric-shock gloves against animals?

Will ICE prohibit the use of the electric-shock gloves in crowd-control situations?

What restrictions will govern the duration and repetition of electrical shocks?

Will the electric-shock gloves be authorized for use against U.S. citizens?

Will the electric-shock gloves be authorized for use in custodial settings? Will they be authorized for use in removal operations?

How will protocol for use differ between HSI and ERO?

Testing, Medical Safety, and Training

What testing has DHS or ICE conducted or reviewed concerning the safety and effectiveness of the electric-shock gloves? Please provide all manufacturer testing, independent testing, medical evaluations, risk assessments, and other relevant documentation.

Will ICE conduct a limited pilot program before broad deployment? If so, provide the parameters, location, duration, and evaluation criteria for the pilot.

What medical contraindications or risks has ICE identified related to use of the electricshock gloves?

What training will be required before an officer or agent may carry or use the electricshock gloves? Please provide all existing and proposed training and written guidance concerning the G.L.O.V.E., including curricula, lesson plans, instructor materials, certification standards, policy directives, field guidance, and manufacturer training materials.

Will ICE require recurring certification and refresher training? Please provide the certification requirements, frequency of recertification, proficiency standards, and consequences for personnel who fail to maintain certification.

Accountability, Reporting, and Oversight

What is the required response when a person is injured or appears to be in medical distress following use of the electric-shock gloves? Please provide the applicable medical response protocols, including requirements for medical evaluation, documentation, notification of supervisors, and preservation of evidence.

Will every activation or use of the electric-shock gloves against a person be reported as a use of force?

Will ICE require body-worn cameras to be activated and operational whenever the electric-shock gloves are deployed, regardless of whether the officers are in plainclothes?

Will every activation require written justification and supervisory review? Please identify who will review these incidents, what factors supervisors must consider, and what specific consequences will apply when personnel violate the applicable restrictions.

How will ICE track complaints and injuries? Will ICE maintain and publicly report data concerning internal and external complaints, injuries, improper uses, disciplinary actions, and uses of force involving the electric-shock gloves?

How will ICE evaluate, track, and report complaints of civil rights violations involving the use of the electric-shock gloves?

Will ICE conduct an independent audit of the program?

Please provide records reflecting any internal concerns or objections regarding the electric-shock gloves, including communications involving the Office of Tactical Programs and Firearms.

text:
A man who claims he was assaulted by ICE agents earlier this month is now asking police to investigate.

José Mejía Hernandez was walking to work in Arlington, Virginia, on Aug. 11 when he says he was approached by two people he did not know were federal agents. He says he tried to run away but the agents assaulted him, resulting in a brain injury.

ICE disputes that account, saying Mejía Hernandez tried to evade arrest and that agents used necessary force to take him into custody.

On Friday, Mejía Hernandez and his attorneys went to Arlington County police headquarters to file a report and are calling for the agents involved to be criminally prosecuted.

Mejía Hernandez’s attorneys say they received video from people who started recording after Mejía Hernandez was taken into custody by federal immigration agents. The video begins with him on the ground, with his face bloody and bruised, but does not show what happened to him to cause the injuries. Minutes later in the video, agents are seen helping Mejía Hernandez to his feet. He appears unsteady as agents surround him before the video ends.

That was 17 days ago. On Friday, Mejía Hernandez appeared with his attorneys outside the Arlington County Police Department, where they filed a police report. His face is still bruised.

He says he can’t sleep, that it’s hard for him to eat and he feels scared. He said he was hospitalized after the incident that he suffered a brain injury. News4 has not been able to independently confirm or review medical documentation that supports this claim.

He says he doesn’t remember what exactly happened after he was stopped by agents, only that he recalls waking up in the hospital.

Mejía Hernandez is from Mexico and is in the United States without documentation.

In the days following the incident, ICE said in a statement sent to News4 that Mejía Hernandez tried to run from the scene, requiring what they called “necessary force” to gain control of the situation. ICE says allegations that he was unconscious and woke up in a hospital bed are false.

ICE did not directly respond to News4's request for comment Friday about Mejía Hernandez's decision to file a police report. Instead, the agency sent us a statement it had previously released.

Meanwhile, Denisse Gastélum, a civil rights attorney representing Mejía Hernandez, asked: “How does a man who is walking to a bus stop on his way to work suddenly wake up with a brain injury at the hands of federal immigration officers?"

"That is not my America," she said.

Supporters of Mejía Hernandez gathered to stand behind him outside police headquarters, holding signs condemning ICE’s actions. His attorneys say they are seeking justice and accountability, while raising concerns about what they call increasingly forceful tactics by immigration authorities.

“Unfortunately, it doesn't seem like the end's coming," said Carlos Jurado, Mejía Hernandez’s immigration attorney. "It seems like these arrests are getting more violent and without answers.”

Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, the commonwealth’s attorney for Arlington County — who decides whether charges could be filed — was in attendance and called the assault allegations concerning.

“It doesn't matter if you're a federal official. It doesn't matter if you're just a regular person on the street," she said. "Everybody must be held accountable. And I will do my utmost to make sure that that happens.”

Arlington County police told News4 that detectives met with Mejía Hernandez, who filed a police report alleging violations of Virginia laws involving aggravated malicious wounding, malicious wounding, failure of driver in accident to stop, reckless driving and assault and battery.

The incident was documented in a police report and the investigation is ongoing, police said.

Mejía Hernandez’s attorneys also say they plan on suing the federal government over the incident and are requesting a U Visa for Mejía Hernandez. A U visa a special kind of visa that can be offered to victims of crimes in the United States, those who help law enforcement investigate or prosecute a crime.

“Our hope is that those federal agents who caused harm to Mr. Mejía Hernandez are held criminally liable,” Gastélum said.

Mejía Hernandez has been placed in deportation proceedings. His attorney says he has an immigration court hearing set for Sept. 14.

text:
PHARR, Texas (Border Report) — The number of denaturalization lawsuits filed by the Trump administration surged in July, according to new data.

There were 50 denaturalization lawsuits filed by the Department of Justice in July, according to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse. That’s the most ever in recent memory.

There were 18 denaturalization cases filed in June, which migrant advocates at the time thought was a whopping number. But now it’s more than doubled.

There were only eight cases filed to strip naturalized citizens of their citizenship in all of 2025. But since January, there have been 105 denaturalization cases filed nationwide.

Lawsuits were filed in 23 states in July alone, TRAC reports.

Florida had the most, with nine cases, followed by seven in Texas; six in Maryland and two in California.

TRAC reports that the number of denaturalization cases might actually be higher because the federal government does not publicize all of its cases.

In June, Democracy FWD filed a challenge in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to compel U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Justice to release public information relating to its plans for denaturalization cases.

Sandra Sanchez can be reached at SSanchez@BorderReport.com.

title: New records detail ICE arrests during summer surge. Yakima, Seattle top the list - KUOW

Just to compare, in just those two months of this year, ICE arrests eclipsed all the recorded arrests during the first seven months of 2025.
The project obtains records of ICE arrests and detentions through Freedom of Information Act requests to the Department of Homeland Security.
Before this summer's surge of ICE arrests and detentions in Seattle, cities like Yakima had already been feeling the significant effects of ramped up immigration enforcement and arrests.

text:
Immigration arrests across Washington state shot up to a new high over the summer, reflecting a nationwide surge in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The newly published records show which cities in Washington state were the hardest hit.

Roughly 700 people were arrested each month in June and July. Just to compare, in just those two months of this year, ICE arrests eclipsed all the recorded arrests during the first seven months of 2025. About 24 people were detained in June and July 2024 during the final year of former President Joe Biden’s term.

Washington hasn’t seen a day without an ICE arrest since late March, according to ICE records. In Seattle, fewer and fewer days also go by without an arrest, often only pausing on the weekend, according to records released this week from the Deportation Data Project based at the University of California and analyzed by KUOW.

The project obtains records of ICE arrests and detentions through Freedom of Information Act requests to the Department of Homeland Security. For the first time, the records published by researchers also now breakdown arrests by city.

From January through the end of July, here are the top cities where people have been arrested.

Yakima: 522 arrests

Seattle: 477 arrests

Tukwila: 362 arrests

Spokane: 342 arrests

After that, cities like in Tacoma, SeaTac, and Kent each have had more than 100 people arrested over the past several months.

Nearly all the arrests take place in the community through traffic stops, at check-ins or other enforcement. The ICE records refer to these as “at large” or street arrests.

A small percentage of arrests, categorized as “custodial arrests” happen through transfers from state or federal prisons to ICE custody. These transfers are a level of state cooperation with immigration enforcement that’s allowed under the Keep Washington Working Act.

According to the data, the majority of street arrests are people who have no criminal record.

Unlike previous and highly visible ICE operations in other states, much of enforcement in Washington is often discreetly happening early in the morning or in the evening hours.

“It felt like we were chasing ghosts,” said David Morales. He leads the immigrant response teams for the Yakima Immigrant Response Network, which has been operating since President Donald Trump’s first term.

Before this summer's surge of ICE arrests and detentions in Seattle, cities like Yakima had already been feeling the significant effects of ramped up immigration enforcement and arrests. Initially it was a challenge for the network’s efforts to document and report ICE arrests to the public.

“It was like trying to find evidence of what had occurred because these things would happen, and all we would have is a smashed car window or a vacant car,” Morales said.

Since then the Yakima network has made strides, including having local content creators help vet reports online, and tracking reports posted to social media.

“Over the course of the last year and a half, we've gotten a bit more community trust, and community members know to record these things. We're able to find recordings of ICE arrests much more commonly than we used to find,” Morales said.

Many of the people arrested in Washington state are taken into custody during a vehicle stop. Along with targeted enforcement, immigration enforcement will use racial profiling, and other factors, to identify someone to arrest while out on patrol. They access driver and license plate records managed by the Washington Department of Licensing and Washington State Patrol, putting those state agencies at odds with state laws that were passed in effort to limit the amount of cooperation between Washington state and federal immigration enforcement agencies.

“There are many victories that turn out to not be victories and not to have any real effect,” Morales said.

The governor's office said there is no immediate way to address this incongruence in the near term. They want to avoid fully shutting off all access to the federal government in order to keep information flowing for public safety concerns — such as law enforcement that targets human trafficking.

Morales also said many arrests are also frequently happening outside of local courts, and points to the Courts Open to All Act, passed the year after the Keep Washington Working Act, as also floundering. That act sought to prevent immigration enforcement from interfering with local court matters.

“It's the same thing with the face mask law [that] has been blatantly violated every single day,” he said. “I think the passage of the law encouraged them to put on the mask as a political signal of rebellion against the state.”

Since last September Morales said the Yakima network has launched a humanitarian department helping families who’ve lost a breadwinner with legal aid, meal boxes, gas cards, and other basic supplies. In some cases they’ve also been helping families secure U.S. and Mexican passports to leave the country if the family chooses to deport together.

“We're… getting basically move-out packages with suitcases and, and, and other similar items,” Morales said. “It's been very difficult for the volunteers, but it's also been very rewarding for the volunteers.”

Enforcement has struck at the sense of safety of many mixed immigration status communities. Morales points to a decrease in community vitality and a reported decline in Latino businesses, the hardest hit community by immigration enforcement in Yakima.

Other cities and communities are also feeling the effects, as Renton Councilmember Carmen Rivera documented in a social media post this week after an encounter with ICE agents.

“if you are an elected official, it is the least that you can do to confront ICE in your neighborhood,” she said. “We have the position, the privilege, and the platform. Eyes are on us, and it is up to us to protect our neighbors.”

Rivera joined a group of her neighbors in a standoff with ICE agents Thursday that lasted 45 minutes, she said. Officers were parked in front of her neighbor’s home in two SUVs with tinted windows, one identified with ICE logo on the side of the vehicle. Inside she said she saw agents with face coverings.

She approached one of the ICE officers asking why they were in her neighborhood. She was told they had a warrant for one of their neighbors who was inside their home.

“ He would not show me this warrant and basically said they would not leave until they were able to serve this warrant, which they were not able to show me,” she posted online.

After 45 minutes, Rivera said the ICE agents left. She said it was a case of mistaken identity. Her neighbor was a U.S. citizen.

But the neighborhood is now vigilant, expecting ICE agents to return. The daughter of a police officer, Rivera said Trump’s immigration enforcement crackdown is not making her community safer.

“ These cowards aren't going to stop. It's gonna be up to us to keep us safe,” she said. “So stay vigilant, stay safe, join a rapid response group if you can, get to know your neighbors, take care of each other, and please be safe.”

text:
The Assembly passed a bill Friday to impose an annual tax on private detention centers, sending the legislation to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk.

Assembly Bill 1633 establishes the Private Detention Facility Tax Law, which would impose an annual 25% tax on operators of private detention centers. The money collected from the tax would be deposited into a “Due Process for All Fund” in the State Treasury, which would finance immigration-related services and support for communities impacted by detention centers.

The legislation passed by a 30-10 vote in the Senate Thursday and a 54-17 vote in the Assembly, both along party lines.

Assemblymember Matt Haney, D-San Francisco, said he authored the bill in reaction to reports of inadequate living conditions in California’s private immigration detention facilities. Allegations of insufficient medical care and lack of hygiene products, edible food and clean drinking water were among these concerns, according to Haney.

“For years, (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) has fueled a system that profits from human suffering and family separation, outsourcing detention to private corporations who rake in profits while people endure dangerous, inhumane conditions,” Haney said in a statement to The Sacramento Bee. “Corporations running these facilities are being paid hundreds of millions to detain people in cruelty right here in California, and it has to end.”

The legislation comes shortly after two private detention facilities opened in California, bringing the state’s total to eight. The California City Immigration Processing Center, which opened in August 2025, is California’s largest immigrant detention facility with 2,560 beds. This April, for-profit prison company Geo Group opened the 700-bed Central Valley Annex facility in McFarland, Calif.

The construction of new detention centers in California is part of President Donald Trump’s nationwide effort to expand ICE arrests and detentions. The Trump administration announced a $45 billion expansion of detention facilities nationwide in February.

“What we’re seeing across the country shows the real-world consequences of ICE’s unchecked power, putting communities and lives at risk for profit with zero accountability,” Haney said.

Opponents to the legislation have said imposing a tax on detention facilities would impede the activities of federal law enforcement officials. Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, voiced his dissent in a May 27 Assembly floor hearing, saying the measure would lead to the closure of immigration detention facilities.

“It unfairly smears and defames the good men and women of federal law enforcement who are just doing their jobs,” DeMaio said. “Not only are you not helping get the criminals out of these communities, you’re gonna release them back into the communities for them to re-commit crimes.”

However, the bill’s supporters maintain the tax would only apply to private civil detention facilities, which do not hold individuals charged with crimes. While the bill would likely impose a fiscal burden on detention facilities, it does not mandate their closure.

“People continue to be detained…with no meaningful end in sight,” said Assemblymember Juan Carrillo, D-Palmdale, during the hearing. “AB 1633 says that if corporations are going to operate detention facilities in California and generate massive revenues from them, they should help pay for the harm and public cost created in our communities.”

The bill has the support of over 100 organizations, including legal aid groups, immigrant rights advocates and community alliances. The bill is co-sponsored by the California Immigrant Policy Center and Services Immigrant Rights Education Network, who advocate for the human rights of detained individuals.

“People have shared stories about their loved ones being denied medical care…and not being able to receive healthy food or adequate water inside the detention centers,” said Shiu-Ming Cheer, deputy director of immigrant and racial justice at the California Immigrant Policy Center. “These facilities are being operated with little to no accountability…it’s really unacceptable. California can and hopefully will do more through this bill to ensure that we protect the rights of Californians.”
